> Known in the Basin as Perry. His true name is Peiric, of the merchant House Castaigne, carried > from his homeland across the western ocean. The Tongue-Guild clipped it to the sound its own tongues > could hold, and "Perry" is what came back; he answers to it. A Tongue-Guild translator in the Aethelian Basin, twenty-seven years old, and one of the few in the crossroads who looks the way he does. He is six foot one, with light brown hair, blue eyes, and light skin, pale among the dark-eyed, brown-skinned peoples of the six civilizations. He is rare here, but not alone in it: the young western route lands a thin, shifting handful of his own coast's sailors at the port where it berths, and he is among the few who stayed. The blue eyes are his rarer mark, uncommon even among his own people and seldom seen in the Basin, though he is not the first to carry them here. He came young. He trained in the Alto observation network as a young man and has kept Alto dates for thirty years, the last twelve of them as the examiner the Pacha-Urco desk calls when a certificate is questioned and the house wants a finding it can stand behind. The first path in each row's last column is the person's fullest treatment. The Caravan Physician's World A physician crossing Veydria in 1300 carries: a humoral or energetic framework for balance, a small travelling case of dried simples and distilled oils, a lancet, a cautery iron, a cupping horn, and bandages. What changes from region to region is not her craft but her eyes: the sign-clusters she recognises, the plants within a day's walk, and the ailments she has been taught to name. Design philosophy: Ecology is real; magic does not touch it. No germ theory, no microscope, no anaesthesia beyond opium/mandrake/hemp/henbane/alcohol, no surgical asepsis beyond wine/vinegar/honey. Childhood mortality is high because it was; chronic illness is common because it was; occupational disease is a moral fact of ordinary work. The Rahab and Arwat rahab (Camelus dromedarius, dromedary pack camel; plural ruhub) and arwat (aristocratic riding breed). Names preserved verbatim — no alteration, no alternative proposed. Co-Evolutionary History The Irrah interior is hyper-arid and forbids any economy that cannot walk from oasis to oasis. The camel's physiology is the solution: oval red blood cells that circulate through dehydrated blood without clumping; selective brain-cooling via the carotid rete; tolerance of 30-40% body-weight water loss; the ability to drink 140 liters in a single session; a fat hump decoupled from water storage; nasal passages that recover exhaled moisture. Two functionally distinct lines from the same species: - rahab — stocky, broad-chested, carrying 150-250 kg at caravan pace for weeks between wells - arwat — light-skeletoned, deep-girthed, "greyhound-bellied," bred for speed and endurance under a single rider The two lines interbreed but the distinction is maintained by ownership lineage. One does not load a known arwat with trade goods; one does not ride a rahab to one's own wedding. Cultural Role The rahab moves desert commerce — salt, dates, textiles, glass, copper — along…

The Tokhan Horse Tokhan (Equus ferus caballus, Mongolian-type landrace). Back-harmony vowels o and a, aspirate kh, final nasal n typical of Kheshkai animate nouns. Plural: tokhat (collective suffix). Phonological note: Revised from original "Turghan" proposal (which contained forbidden /r/). Tokhan uses back-harmony /o/ + /a/ with no liquid consonants. Co-Evolutionary History The Kheshkai steppe swings from -40 C winter to +40 C summer, and the tokhan survives the full swing without shelter. Small (12-14 hands), stocky, thick-coated, hard-hooved, it paws through snow for winter grass, tolerates dehydration, and needs no shoeing. Selection for hardiness, foraging self-sufficiency, and endurance over speed — mediocre sprinter, extraordinary distance animal (60-80 miles/day when remounted). The composite recurve bow is usable from the saddle only because the tokhan is trainable to respond to knee pressure. Conversely, the bow made the tokhan the state's strategic asset. Each fighting man keeps 3-5 remounts on campaign, with preference for lactating mares (airag-analog dairy always at hand). The Ndowu Buffalo Ndowu (Bubalus bubalis, water buffalo — swamp type). Prenasalized nd- onset, round back vowel o, open u final. Tone: low-high (ndo-wu). Plural: bandowu by class-prefix. Co-Evolutionary History The Ndjadi delta alternates deep-flood and cracked-clay drawdown, and the ndowu is the only bovid that thrives across the full cycle. Splayed hooves and flexible pasterns let it plow belly-deep mud where any cow would founder; sparse sweat glands make wallowing obligate. Centuries of selection for draft power over dairy yield produced a stocky swamp-type animal — smaller than upland river-type dairy buffalo, but tractable, surefooted in paddy, and long-lived. The ndowu's true agronomic gift is puddling: repeated passes under yoke churn flooded topsoil into a compacted plow-pan that seals the field against percolation, multiplying the value of every unit of irrigation water. Without the ndowu, the delta's wet-rice economy does not run at scale. A pair is the practical minimum for a tenant household; a team of four marks a landed family. The Longa Cattle Longa (Bos taurus africanus, Sanga-type cattle of the Nguni lineage). The everyday stock-name takes plain pulmonic onsets; the lateral fricative and click that an earlier draft stacked into the word (hl-, nq-) belong to the Gyamsgra sacred forge-register and do not surface in common cattle-names. Noun-class plural: iziLonga (many cattle), uLonga (a single named beast). Co-Evolutionary History Descended from ancient Sanga hybridization of taurine and humped stocks. Characteristic cervico-thoracic hump (muscular, set forward), lyre-shaped horns, short glossy coat in hundreds of named patterns, and tolerance for tick-borne disease, heat, and drought no imported breed matches. Selection primarily for hardiness and coat-pattern beauty rather than raw milk yield or carcass weight — a herd is read as a living textile. The mixed woodland-savanna ecology rewards a browsing-tolerant grazer that moves between grass and scrub and survives seasonal drought on body reserves. Longa's central economic role: the interest-bearing capital of the lineage — they reproduce, move, and bind families through transfer. Cultural Role Longa are bride-wealth made animate. Marriage…

The Naluma Tree Naluma (Artocarpus altilis, breadfruit). Strict open-syllable CV-CV-CV, low back vowel a with rounded u break, liquid l. No consonant clusters, no closed syllables. A cultivar is a naluma; a grove or lineage-orchard is a nalumarai. Co-Evolutionary History Austronesian colonists carried breadfruit along every leg of the archipelagic expansion because a single adult tree can feed a household for fifty years on almost no labor once established. Clonal propagation from root suckers let founders move selected varieties onto new volcanic islands within a generation of landfall. Centuries of selection produced scores of cultivars distinguished by fruit season, flesh texture, seed-bearing vs. seedless, and trunk straightness and latex yield. The tree solved four problems at once: staple starch, canoe timber, caulking gum, and bast fiber for cordage and tapa-analog cloth. No other Oravan cultivar is simultaneously food, hull, and glue. The Q'awa Camelid Q'awa (Lama glama, llama). Initial ejective uvular /q'/ — the Qollari signature sound. Back low vowel a, open CV final. Plural by reduplication: q'awaq'awa for a drove, q'awakuna with plural suffix. Co-Evolutionary History The Qollari altiplano is too high for the horse, too cold for the ox, and too steep for the wheeled cart. The q'awa resolves all three problems. Bred from the wild guanaco over four to five millennia, it evolved for cloud-forest and puna pastoralism at 3,500-4,500 m. Its soft two-toed pad puts negligible pressure on fragile ichu-grass soils; high-affinity hemoglobin lets it work above 5,000 m; low water demand matches a glacial-stream landscape. Selection pressure has been for pack endurance over speed: carries 25-30% of body weight 15-20 km/day across passes no mule could cross. Two parallel lineages bred alongside: a finer-boned fiber variant (alpaca analog) and a state-protected wild fiber giver (vicuna analog). Cultural Role The q'awa is the state's logistical spine and religious offering of first choice. He is reading the grain-drift — the faint striae that every wind-reader knows. He tastes the air for the metallic dryness that foretells qibli, the harmattan-analog dust wind. Today: cold, clean, dry. A winter crossing. Good. In the staging-yard the ruhub groan as the packers heave salt-slabs — each roughly the size of a tombstone, two to a rahab — and lash them with plaited palm-rope. Breath steams. A Seven-Day Crossing of the Kheshkai The first light over the Kheshkai Steppe is not light but cold — a blue, breath-stinging cold that bites even in the Grass Moon of high summer. You wake inside the felt tent to the bitter sweetness of dung smoke — argal, dried sheep and horse pats layered into the central iron stove — and the sour-milk damp of the airag skin swinging from the door-frame, punched by every passer-by to keep it churning. The felt walls, bone-white with chalk on the outside, are warm as a lung within. You step out right-footed — never onto the threshold, which steppe custom calls the neck of the house, and which it is ruinous to tread. Horses are already nosing a seep where dark water wells through Carex sedge and pale rye-grass (Leymus), and the men water them in turns, whistling low; somewhere a Siberian marmot (Marmota sibirica) whistles its own sharp alarm from a burrow-mound crowned in silvery wormwood (Artemisia frigida). Before riding out, the three-bowl protocol: milk-tea, then aaruul (dried curd), then fermented mare's milk. You take it with the right hand, left hand cupping the right elbow. You flick three drops — sky, wind, earth — before you drink.…

Pied kingfishers hover; a Nile monitor (Varanus niloticus) slides from a mudbank like poured oil. Pirogues arrow out from the reed screens, offering smoked bonga and green oysters knotted on vine. Passage Through the Archipelago The first watch of a dry-monsoon morning breaks grey over the anchorage. Before the sun lifts above the palms, the lagoon is a sheet of pewter; you hear the village before you see it — the thump-thump-thump of an outrigger paddle on a hollow hull as a fisherman scares baitfish, the wet slap of a net cast, a rooster on the beach answering another across the channel, and from somewhere in the coconut grove (Cocos nucifera), the ratcheting call of hornbills and the argument of lorikeets in a flowering Syzygium. A Llama Caravan on the Qhapaq Nan — Five Days Vertical Day One — Yungas. You set out before dawn from the cloud-forest tambo where the paved road begins its climb out of the valley. The air is warm and wet, black with the smell of wet moss. The Three Master Constraints Three ecological constraints do most of the work in driving continental trade: 1. Irrah's timber absence is the continent's single largest trade driver. No wood means no charcoal means no primary iron, forcing the desert into permanent dependence on Ngaru-Bon bloomeries and making the iron-north/salt-south axis of trans-desert caravan trade structurally inevitable. This is the Saharan reality, not a worldbuilding flourish. 2. The tsetse barrier silently shapes Ngaru-Bon's military and logistical profile. A metallurgical apex with no cavalry and severe pack-transport limits exports gold and iron but cannot project force, pushing its trade outward through the Swahili-coast analog rather than overland. 3. Point-source biota — clove on five islands, nutmeg on one archipelago, vicuna above 3,800 m, frankincense on specific fog-fed escarpments — create monopoly rents that fund entire civilizations. These monopolies are inherently fragile; a single bad volcanic year in Oravan or a failed monsoon on Dhofar would reshape continental politics. What the Basin Produces The Basin produces almost no commodity and governs the movement of nearly all of them. Its economy is institutional arbitrage, the sale of services that turn a stateless delta into the continent's single clearing house, and enumerates five. The warehouse-keeper guilds hold goods through their seasons, storing grain eighteen months, cotton three years, and spices indefinitely, and they are paid in the commodity stored, accumulating diversified portfolios without ever trading. The khazadari money-changer guild sets the daily cross-rates between salt-weight, iron-weight, cotton-weight, grain-measure, and silver-by-weight. The triple-seal panels arbitrate contracts. The tithe-operators sell insurance. The investor dynasties structure partnerships. What the Basin sells is not a thing but a guarantee: that a good can be aged and released against monsoon timing, that an oath will be enforced, that a loss at sea or in the desert will be made good. The five guilds hold mixed, multi-civ membership, which is the mechanism that keeps the clearing house neutral, because any visible bias would trigger defection by the disadvantaged civilization. What Irrah Produces Irrah holds the continent's rock-salt monopoly, and the monopoly is the load-bearing fact of its economy. The sabkha slabs cut from its salt-flats, the Taghaza and Taoudenni analog of Veydria, are the most universally accepted inland commodity money on the continent, and the salt itself is the northern anchor of the continental spine against Ndjadi grain. Around the salt, the drylands yield natron, dates, lode silver from Jabali-analog deposits, impact-silica glass, and medicinal gums from the Sahel-margin thorn-savanna. A second export cluster sits on the southeastern coast: frankincense and myrrh from a Dhofar-analog shore, the resin trade that gives Irrah a maritime outlet entirely independent of the Basin. Irrah also breeds the camel stock the desert trade runs on, rahab pack-animals and arwat riding-camels, and it sells the crossing itself. The caravan is the product as much as the cargo, and Qalībin escort and certification are billed services in their own right. What Irrah Cannot Make Irrah has no timber, and timber is the dependency that organizes its weaknesses. Without wood there is no charcoal, and without charcoal there is no sustained bloomery,…

What Kheshkai Produces Kheshkai sells two things the continent cannot do without and a third that is the trade itself. The first is warhorses and remounts, the only cavalry-grade source at scale on the continent, an export that confers military capability no settled neighbor can manufacture. The second is tin, drawn from a Zeravshan-analog source so geologically rare that two or three nodes supply the whole continent, and tin is half of bronze. Because Ngaru-Bon copper cannot become bronze without it, Kheshkai tin underwrites the steppe's political autonomy as surely as its horses underwrite its raids. Around these the steppe exports felt and wool, furs, amber, hides and sinew, and livestock on the hoof. The third product is protection: the rent a caravan pays for safe passage, the steppe selling the absence of its own predation. Horse, tin, and protection are the levers, and each one binds a settled civilization that would rather not need the steppe at all. What Kheshkai Cannot Make The steppe cannot grow grain. Rainfall below three hundred millimeters cannot support plow agriculture at the population scales a nomad confederation reaches, and herds give dairy and meat but no…

What Ndjadi Produces Ndjadi is the breadbasket of Veydria, and that single fact organizes everything else about its economy. The floodplain produces a continental staple surplus in wheat, barley, millet, and rice, the only bulk-carbohydrate output on the continent large enough to feed populations that cannot feed themselves. The surplus exists because the river floods on a predictable cycle and deposits new alluvium each season, a renewable fertility that needs no fallow and no manure. Around the grain sits a second tier of floodplain products: cotton cloth and raw cotton from the irrigated margins, a papyrus-analog for the scribal trade, dried river-fish, indigo, flax and linen, natron, and ceramics fired from delta clay. Ndjadi also exports copper drawn from upstream-margin deposits on the Sinai-analog edge of its territory, and that copper is the primary feed for the Ngaru-Bon bronze trade along the Copper-for-Steel Road. None of these are point-source monopolies in the way Oravan obsidian or Irrah salt are. Ndjadi's leverage is bulk and reliability: it sells the one commodity four other civilizations must buy or starve. What Ndjadi Cannot Make The delta is rich in soil and…

What Ngaru-Bon Produces Ngaru-Bon is the metallurgical apex of the continent. Its bloomeries produce iron bars of a quality no other civilization can match, its crucibles produce steel ingots that exist nowhere else at scale, and its smiths turn out finished work that the whole continent buys: chainmail, curved blades, architectural supports. The plateau also exports copper from Katanga-analog deposits, ivory, and gold, though gold occupies a category of its own. What makes Ngaru-Bon's position singular is not the volume of its metal but the absence of competitors. Iron and steel are existential to most settled civilizations and critical to all of them, and the plateau is the source. Where Ndjadi sells a bulk commodity that four neighbors need to eat, Ngaru-Bon sells a finished good that the same neighbors need to farm, fight, and build, and it sells it without any second supplier to discipline its terms. What Ngaru-Bon Cannot Make The plateau cannot keep a horse. The tsetse belt that surrounds its approach corridors causes nagana in any draft or cavalry animal that tries to cross, which means the continent's greatest forge has no force-projection capability whatsoever. records…

What Oravan Produces Oravan trades in things that grow nowhere else. The volcanic archipelago holds two point-source monopolies: obsidian, the sharpest cutting edge available to civilizations without universal iron access, drawn from five islands, and the deep-sea spices, clove and nutmeg and mace, endemic to a handful of islands and a single archipelago cluster. To these the islands add pumice, coral-stone blocks for architecture, cured fish, teak and belian hardwoods, pearl, tortoiseshell, and sandalwood. The spice and obsidian trades are what give Oravan its weight on the continent, because both are genuinely irreplaceable: there is no second source of clove, and obsidian's precision edge is needed even by Ngaru-Bon, whose iron is too soft for the finest work. Oravan's wealth is the wealth of a monopoly holder. It is also the wealth of a monopoly holder whose entire stock can be destroyed by a single bad season. What Oravan Cannot Make Oravan has no iron and no bog ore. The andesitic and basaltic volcanics of the archipelago are ore-poor, so every nail, every fish-hook, and every ship-anchor is imported, and names iron as the irreplaceable dependency. The dependency is…

What Qollari Produces Qollari sells altitude. Its highland exports are high in value and low in bulk: medicinal bark, the cinchona-analog fever-bark that no lowland can grow, rare dyestuffs of the cochineal kind, and the fine camelid fiber, vicuna-analog above 3,800 meters, that constitutes a wool monopoly the lowlands cannot touch. To these the cloud-states add structural timber from the wetter slopes, silver, gold, processed tin-bronze worked from imported Kheshkai tin, and freeze-dried chuno that keeps for years. The economy is built around goods whose worth per kilogram is high enough to justify carriage by an animal that refuses to be overloaded. Qollari does not compete in bulk staples; it competes in the irreplaceable and the rare, the fever-bark a dying merchant will pay anything for, the dye a priestess-queen's robe requires, the fiber that no flock below the snow-line can produce. What Qollari Cannot Make Qollari cannot feed itself. The terraces raise tubers and a quinoa-analog, but they cannot produce bulk carbohydrates at altitude in the quantities a population needs, and names grain as the irreplaceable dependency. The highlands must buy Ndjadi grain, and there is…

The Continental Spine Revisited The whole Veydrian order bends around two axes that ecology made inevitable. The first is Grain against Salt. Ndjadi alluvium floods and refertilizes itself each season and produces the only bulk-carbohydrate surplus on the continent, while it raises neither salt, nor metal, nor stone, nor timber. Irrah sabkha yields the only continental rock-salt and stands on a desert with no tree from which to draw charcoal. Four civilizations cannot feed themselves without Ndjadi grain, and the same four and their herds cannot survive without Irrah salt. Neither the breadbasket nor the salt-pan can ever supply what the other holds, and so the two ends of the continent are locked into a dependence that no innovation will dissolve. The second axis is metallurgical: bronze requires Kheshkai tin from two or three rare nodes joined to Ngaru-Bon copper, and iron and steel come from the Ngaru-Bon plateau alone. The spine is not a trade pattern that happened to form. It is the shape the continent must take given where the salt, the grain, the tin, and the ore actually lie, and every other flow bends around it. The Complementary-Asymmetry Principle The Veydrian economy rests on a single structural fact: no civilization can supply itself, and every civilization holds at least one thing that no other civilization can substitute. The six settled powers and the Aethelian Basin do not trade because trade is profitable at the margin. They trade because the alternative is collapse. Ndjadi grows grain on an alluvium that yields no metal, no salt, no stone, and no timber. Irrah holds the only continental rock-salt monopoly while owning not a single tree from which to make the charcoal its forges would require. Ngaru-Bon stands at the metallurgical apex of the continent and cannot keep a horse alive past the tsetse belt that walls its approaches. The dependencies are not soft preferences; they are listed in as irreplaceable, civilization by civilization, and each one binds its holder to a named supplier whose leverage is structural rather than negotiable. Value in this system is created at borders, not at sources. Institutional Substrate Kheshkai is "Non-institutional" in the typology of magic/06, the only Veydrian civ at this position on the Schism Axis. There are no colleges, no guilds, no lineages in the formal sense; master-shamans take one to three apprentices over a five-to-ten-year horseback apprenticeship; identification is by the hearing-gift, a phonological capacity detectable in childhood. Orthodoxy does not survive a master's death unmediated. Every shaman is a potential single point of failure, and every harmonic pattern is one bad transmission from extinction. The consequence is fragility. Institutional Substrate Ngaru-Bon is "Monolithic" in the typology of magic/06, the only Veydrian civ at this position on the Schism Axis. Fracture Substrate The Ngaru-Bon calendar is held not in months or years but in the names of the smiths who hold tier-credentials. The ancestor-smith tiers — Nokul (initiate), Amori (master), Lapam (ancestor) — are temporal coordinates. A tier promotion closes one generation and opens another; the date is inscribed in the forge-temple's click-register ledger, the only written calendar the Ngaru-Bon maintain. The Outside-Forge Network uses the same tier names but refuses the Inner Council's promotion authority. The Network's "Amori Phyi-Ma" may be the same mortal who held the name twenty years ago, or a successor who inherited the name, or a fiction the Network maintains for contractual continuity. A warehouse clerk brought the certified tally to a side-table, watched while he worked, and entered in the room-log that the examiner had handled it. Nothing left the room. That was the regime, and it was the regime that made the room worth coming to: a registered cord kept under the warehouse's own hand could not be quietly swapped for a friendlier one. He read the certified tally first, alone, before he set the certificate beside it. A finding that the certificate had been shifted was worth nothing…

The reading-room and the wharf, Ki-Mbuhari, two days before the hearing --- The Alto delegate came to the reading-room without sending word ahead, which a senior man of the Concordance did not do unless he wanted the meeting unrecorded. Wata-Niy knew his rank by the cliff-road braid on his coat before he knew his face. The delegate did not sit. He asked, in plain Alto speech, whether the examiner had reached a count, and Wata-Niy, who had kept Alto dates for thirty years and did not lie to the Concordance, said that he had. Nine days. The middle course cut and re-tied. The delegate said that the Concordance already knew. The practice had run two cycles, and the Concordance had come by its own proof of it. Then he said the rest of it, which Wata-Niy had not known and did not want. To publish a finding of backdating against the Upriver keeper would open a restitution proceeding, and a restitution proceeding would put the Concordance's own records into the Court, and in those records was a second house, an Alto-aligned trade family, that shifted its own certificates the same way, at its own seasons, and that the Concordance permitted to do so because the permission was a leash.…

The Triple-Seal Court's Ki-Mbuhari sitting, the hearing day --- The Court sat in a notarial hall the copy-houses kept for it, the prefix-grammar of a hundred cleared contracts stamped into the registers along the walls. Wata-Niy sat in the examiner's place to the side, where a man who had filed an instrument waited in case the bench wanted him, and was not called. The house had submitted his leaf the evening before, as part of its demand. The clerk had taken it under the deferred matter and read its two measurements into the day's record without adopting them. A finding became, at that moment, a thing other men used. The Pacha-Urco factor used it first. He stood with the house's grievance and read the examiner's leaf aloud to the bench, the count course cut and re-tied, the window short of the certified tally by nine days, and he let the two measurements stand as what they were and then named them what the house needed them to be. An Upriver-aligned keeper had falsified a certificate to rob an Alto-aligned house of a season's bark, and here was the count, sworn by a keeper of thirty years, and the house demanded restitution from the Upriver Confederation. Wata-Niy listened to…

Wawa-Kocha observatory compound, the registration chamber, two days before opening session --- The registration chamber occupied the ground floor of the eastern annex. Below the observation galleries and above the altitude where the cliff-road caravans stopped, the chamber was warm in the way that high-altitude rooms were warm when they had been built correctly: thick walls, a low ceiling, a hearth in the corner. The Wawa-Kocha compound had been at this altitude longer than either calendar lineage had a continuous record of occupying it. This was not a fact that either lineage published in its almanacs. Yaqucha had been at the Double-Keepers' registration table since the second hour, before the lineage delegations arrived. The brief folder held seven source-document sets, one per disputed intercalation date in the current cool-season window. Each set required a technical-reconciliation brief: source documents collated, discrepancies characterized, the brief attested by a registered calendar-competent clerk before the session's technical docket opened. She was the Double-Keepers' Technical Secretary for the session. Authorized to prepare and submit technical instruments, to…

Wawa-Kocha compound, the technical working room, first day of session --- The technical working room adjoined the plenary chamber on the compound's western side. Both lineage delegations had deposited their source documents with the session's administrative staff on the first morning; by the second hour the materials had been collated by register and handed to the Double-Keepers' table in the format the session's standing rules required: one bound set per disputed date, numbered in the docket order the standing rules assigned rather than the calendar order of the dates, each set containing the Alto Concordance's written almanac extract, the Upriver Confederation's cord-record, and a notation line reserved for the Double-Keepers' parallel determination. Both lead delegates were in the room. There were no rules against this. The session's standing rules required only that technical consultation between delegations be conducted through the session's administrative staff and that any direct communication between delegates be logged by the chair's recording-clerk. Mbu-Ulinzi ra-Halani was at a desk in the far corner with his logbook open and his pen ready. Neither delegate had said…

Wawa-Kocha compound, the session archive room, second day of session --- The session archive was on the second floor of the eastern annex, above the registration chamber. She submitted a formal access request on the second morning for the Upriver Confederation's primary-evidence records: the cord-recordings of the spring-equinox observation that brief five's source documents cited as the computational basis for the Upriver intercalation claim. The administrative clerk retrieved the bundle and logged the access in the standard form. The records were five cord-lengths sealed in the Confederation's archival wrap, the Sapa Mayu sub-cluster mark on the outer seal, unopened since submission. She broke the seal in the archive room with the administrative clerk present, as the access protocol required, and spread the five cords on the reading table. The cord-lengths were Old Upriver form. The knotting style was pre-schism: the three-cord base with the supplementary quipu running perpendicular to the primary, the configuration her mother's family had been using for household accounts since her grandmother's time, before anyone had found a reason to argue about which observatory's…

Wawa-Kocha compound, the working area and outer chamber, second day of session --- Three paths. She named them on the walk from the archive room back to the Double-Keepers' working area, because naming them was how she worked through problems she had not been trained to solve. The first path: complete the briefs as the submitted records stood. Brief five would document the eleven-day discrepancy between the Upriver cord-record and the Alto almanac extract, cite the Confederation's primary-evidence bundle as the computation basis, and characterize the discrepancy in the category of competing-observatory-jurisdiction disagreements. Which was true, as a category. The four-day error in the fifth cord would sit in the session archive as part of the Upriver submission. When Chaski-Run Hina-Yaq's delegation presented the cord-bundle in plenary session, Inti-Pacha's delegation would have their written almanac extract for the same date. The eleven-day gap was the Schism; both lineages had argued it for three cycles and would argue it for three more. The four-day gap was different. The cord's calculation sat four days below the Sapa Mayu observatory's own historical record, and a…

Wawa-Kocha compound, the working area and plenary chamber, final day of session --- The chair's response arrived in the Double-Keepers' correspondence tray on the third morning: a single page in Mbu-Bwana ra-Kilomba's hand, addressed to the Double-Keepers' Technical Secretary. The Court had received her procedural query. The Court recorded her notation in the session record. Submitted documents were accepted as submitted under the session's standing rules. Any notations concerning technical inconsistencies in submitted records would be held in the session archive pending the next triennial Wawa-Kocha cycle. The page was counter-signed by Mbu-Ulinzi ra-Halani and bore the Court's session stamp. She read it twice. Then she opened the brief folder. The five remaining briefs took the morning. She worked through them in order: collation tables completed, each lineage's position documented, each discrepancy noted without resolution, each brief attested in the two required notations. Brief five documented the eleven-day discrepancy and cited the Upriver primary-evidence bundle as the computation basis. Her procedural-query citation number was in the brief's technical apparatus,…

Tavakh-Qarat, the Tongue-Guild's moral-correspondence overflow room, third day after the triple-seal hold --- The surge work was not regular contract translation. Regular contract translation was Halu-Tabbaq's domain: commercial-oath rendering, witness-clause nuance, the precision work the Guild priced at the top of its schedule. Surge work was what the Senior Council assigned when the moral-correspondence circuit overflowed, and the circuit had been overflowing since the Vernacular-Habal pamphlets started moving at volume. Ki-Vita had been assigned to the overflow room at the third hour. The stack on the table was forty-six documents: Vernacular-Habal pamphlets requiring incoming collation, counter-pamphlet inserts from the Frankincense Syndics requiring formula review, and four certified-response packages that needed a Ṣāliqūn rendering note before the circuit sent them on. Forty-six documents at the standard moral-correspondence apprentice rate credited one khatti per certified rendering. The math was the only encouraging thing in the room. The bond stood at thirty-three khatti when she sat down; the surge had taken nine off it since the triple-seal morning. The…

Ki-Mbuhari, the eastern loading dock, midday --- The secondment errand was a certified-delivery run: three sealed packets from the Tongue-Guild correspondence station at Tavakh-Qarat to the receiving desk at the Halani-Tamu factor house on Ki-Mbuhari's eastern dock. Factor-house certified delivery was standard apprentice work. It did not pay toward the bond. It was what the Guild assigned when the overflow room was caught up and there was nothing else on the contract schedule. The Ki-Mbuhari docks smelled of grain and salt and the particular warm-rot of wet timber that had been wet and dried and wet again over many seasons. The eastern dock was the smaller one, away from the Oravan hull-registration posts and the Harbor Covenant's inspector stations that lined the main quay. Halani-Tamu factor houses clustered on the eastern side for the same reason the transit reinsurance houses did: lower inspection rates, fewer jurisdictional feet on the pier. She found the parchment in the gap between the second and third crates in the loading stack nearest the factor-house door. She almost missed it. The crate gap was a standard receipt position; the Guild's courier protocol listed it as…

Ki-Mbuhari, the reinsurance row and the Tongue-Guild correspondence station, two hours after nightfall --- Three doors. She had named them in her head on the walk back from the passageway, before she had decided anything, because naming them was how she worked through problems that were not translation problems: give each option a door and then stand in front of each one long enough to know what you would be doing if you opened it. The first door was the factor-house address where the tier-sub mark said a ka-tier notary was on secondment. She did not know the specific building. She knew the street from the secondment notice in the family correspondence: the Halani-Tamu reinsurance row, eastern side, six doors from the dock-lane. The door existed and the person behind it was real and the parchment in her folio had been built to be found near him. She did not know what it was staged to accompany. Nothing she could construct was good, and every version she constructed ended with an Irrah chain on the floor beside whatever was found there. Opening the first door meant a warning delivered directly. It also meant arriving at a stranger's factor-house residence at the second hour of…

Tavakh-Qarat, the Triple-Seal Arbitration Court's biennial review room, fourth week after the triple-seal hold --- The certification track was on the room's west side, separate from the Court's main procedural tables. This was the standard arrangement: the biennial review session handled both the docket matters and the Guild's certification queue, the latter in a side alcove behind a low rail that kept it technically outside the Court's formal proceedings. The certification queue moved faster than the docket. It always did. Ki-Vita had been in the queue since the second hour. She had her record folio, her completed rendering tallies for the moral-correspondence surge work, and two counter-signatures: Halu-Tabbaq ult Pulino's on the professional record and Wa-Kande Gser-Dag's on the Basin certification endorsement. The endorsement had arrived at the overflow room four days after her correspondent's notice, carried in the basin-port seat's standard routing packet. It bore Gser-Dag's personal seal and one annotation in the margin: Moral-correspondence retention, next cycle, standard circuit rate. Retention meant she would spend the next working cycle rendering overflow…

Tavakh-Qarat, the warehouse-keeper guild's certification room, first hour after dawn --- The seventh stroke is the one that certifies. Seven strokes per document, and the seventh must be made without lifting the pen: wrist kept low, ink trailing the nib so the line lies flat rather than folding. The Guild called the full cadence the Filer's Hand. Ki-Vita had folded twice in her second year and once in her third. In the year since her third-year examination, she had not folded. She finished the stroke and handed the page to Halu-Tabbaq ult Pulino, who received it without looking. Halu-Tabbaq's eyes were on the document coming through the door: a roll under the arm of a junior warehouse clerk, sealed three times. Ki-Vita counted the seals automatically. Oravan hull-and-cargo first, the raised-anchor pressing. Qalībin water-authority second, the stylized well. Ndjadi scribal-jurisdiction third, the prefix-mark of the ki-tier that was Ki-Vita's own father's mark, the mark that had been in her name since birth. The clerk laid the document on the table and produced a witness-challenge form. "Three today," he said. "All received by the third hour yesterday." Three challenges for a…

Reading Discipline A-Tzalan is the ford where the Kheshkai cliff-edge comes down to the Ndjadi delta, the one overland crossing between the steppe and the floodplain, and the discipline of this file is to describe it as a place whose whole value is conditional on water — crossable or not, held or not, weaponized or not, by the depth of the river in a given season and the will of whoever stands on the bank. The prose stays in the register of the weighed toll and the water-record: how deep the ford runs at low water and when it drowns, which seasons admit only a seized crossing, what holding the ford together with the works upstream did to the delta's harvests, in what coin the toll is taken and to whose account. It does not reach for the register of the river-crossing romance. The water is a real river and a real drowner of the careless, and it is also a lever that has starved a civilization for three growing seasons, and the second fact is the one the records were built to keep. The name is one of the few chokepoints whose etymology the canon preserves, and it preserves the plainest possible one. In the Kheshkai palette the place is A-Tzalan, a "water" and tzalan "crossing" —…

Reading Discipline The Aethelian Basin is a semi-enclosed sea ringed by port-cities, and it is also the place where every civilization on the continent goes to be paid — and the discipline of this file is to describe the second fact as the register of the cross-rate and the seal keeps it, not as the cosmopolitan marvel the prose wants it to be. The Basin invites the marvelling register the way no pass does: six building traditions in one block, six languages in one market, the whole continent's phenotypes blended in one crowd. All of that is true and none of it is what this file keeps. What this file keeps is the working of the institution the Basin is: how value is rated and by whom, who certifies a contract and who may not, what each of the four port-holds funnels into circulation, and why a sea that belongs to no one is the most expensive ground on the continent to be excluded from. Two things in particular live next door and are not retold here. The theology of the contested sites in the Basin's water — Qhabal-Ur's drowned step, the ash-oracle at Veyd-Kirrha, the prefix-dispute at the Ndjadi confluence — belongs to and is pointed to, not re-argued; this file states only how…

Reading Discipline The four port zones of the Basin — Ki-Mbuhari, Tavakh-Qarat, Halani-Tamu, Dzong-Tamu — are not founded on bare ground. Each was built on, into, and through the foundations of what was there before, and what was there before was built on the same logic over the foundations of what was there before that. The present file describes the substrate as a stratigraphic and administrative fact, not as an evocation. Basin merchants pump the lower-stratum cisterns on a fixed schedule, file the expense receipts with the warehouse-master, and route around the unstable courses where the engineering-records have lapsed. Ḥarrāb townsfolk in Tavakh-Qarat speak of ḥawḍ al-aslāf in the same tone they speak of guild dues. The substrate is bureaucratic before it is anything else. The discipline of this file is to keep that tone. The substrate is not haunted; it is leaky, expensive, and contested. When the prose names a foundation as inherited from a vanished culture, the prose stays in the register of the warehouse-master's expense schedule, not the register of the antiquarian's preface. Where the substrate carries a metaphysical claim — the Pacha-Urco householders at Dzong-Tamu…

Reading Discipline Apu-Yana is the Qollari sacred and dangerous peak on the eastern border, and what makes it structurally interesting is that it is named as a warning as much as a landmark — Apu mountain, Yana black, the Black Mountain. The Qollari regard it with both reverence and avoidance, and the discipline of this file is to keep both registers simultaneously: the peak is sacred, and the peak is dangerous, and the two are not separate qualities but a single fact read two ways. It marks the edge of Qollari territory not because any treaty says so but because the cloud forest ends where the volcanic ash begins, and the Qollari hold the forest while the mountain holds itself. What this file keeps is the register of the border and the warning, not the theology of the sacred fire or the ritual calendar that governs approach. The Peak and What It Marks Apu-Yana rises on the eastern margin of the Qollari highlands, where the cloud forest thins and the volcanic zone begins, and its blackness is literal — basalt slopes, ash fields, lava flows that have cooled to a surface too dark for the usual highland vegetation. The Qollari name it plainly: the Black Mountain. The plainness is…

Reading Discipline ʕAyn-Ṣalqat is a place that is mostly a court. Other oases are towns that happen to seat institutions; this one is an institution that happens to have a spring, and the discipline of this file is to keep that order of priority straight. The Covenant Spring is where the founding inter-clan oath of the Irrah confederation was sworn, where the high Qalībin water-court sits, and where the Scribal Ladder pilgrimage reaches its terminus, and almost everything else true of the place follows from one of those three facts. The prose stays in the register of the docket and the certification-filing — what is reviewed, on what cycle, by whom, and what the ruling costs the parties who must obey it — and not in the register of the shrine. One documented fact governs the reading throughout: ʕAyn-Ṣalqat is not on the map. Of the six oasis-cities the confederation records, it is the one absent from the merchant schematic, with no marker on the positions the caravans navigate by. The file does not assert that the Qalībin withhold the coordinate; it reads the absence the way the institutions do, as the natural condition of a place that is reached by those with standing to…

Reading Discipline Breath-of-Cloud is the border where the Kheshkai steppe meets the Qollari cloud forest, and it is also the only permanent joint cross-civ sanctuary on the continent — and the discipline of this file is to describe the border and leave the sanctuary to religion. Why the two peoples meet here, what they recognize in the sky, how the one rite reads the Sky-Witness in two names, and why the convergence of two calendars is the theological content rather than a coincidence — all of that belongs to and is not retold here. What this file keeps is the register of the corridor-account and the rate-slip: that the passage between steppe and highland opens on a calendar and not on the weather, that it opens once in three years and is a dirt track the rest of the time, what the eight days of opening do to the towns that live for them, and what a trade that pays one year in three does to the house that banks it. The reverent register is the named hazard here, more than at any pass, because Breath-of-Cloud is a sanctuary and the prose wants to rise to it. It does not rise to it. The sanctuary is described in this file only as the fixed point a calendar swings a…

Reading Discipline Dzong-Kha is the clan-toll waystation at the foot of Lam-Chen Pass, where Ngaru-Bon and Kheshkai territory effectively meet, and its structural function is to enforce the Blood-Oath — the cross-cultural founding compact that makes the pass usable by both peoples. It is both a waystation and a customs point: stone corrals hold the pack animals that have come down the scree, ice-cellars keep the cisterns from freezing, and a small forge-temple maintains the fire that the compact requires. What this file keeps is the register of the joint authority: how the tariff-rolls are held by neither people alone, how the waystation's governance is the Blood-Oath in physical form, and how the pass stays open only so long as both parties maintain their half of the arrangement. The theology of the forge-rite belongs to religion; the geography records only that the temple is here and that its fire is one of the conditions of passage. The Fortress and What It Tolls Dzong-Kha sits at the southern foot of Lam-Chen Pass, where the Ngaru-Bon plateau's scree gives way to the Kheshkai steppe's grass, and the waystation is built in the Ngaru-Bon fortress-monastery style — heavy stone…

Reading Discipline Dzong-Tamu is the southeast port of the Aethelian Basin, the door by which the Ngaru-Bon plateau's metal enters the continent's circulation, and this file keeps the register of the assay and the guild-mark, not the fortress-gloom of the smallest and most guarded of the four ports. It is the most Ngaru-Bon place that is not the plateau — heavy stone walls, narrow windows, smithy chimneys, the Iron Keep over the skyline — and the architecture is the texture, not the subject. The subject is that new metal reaches the Basin through one certified door and only one, that the door certifies the metal's purity and traces its lineage before it will let it pass, and that the trade is conducted in a register an outsider cannot speak. The forge-rites and the ancestor-claims of the metal belong to the Ngaru-Bon's own families and are not this file's; what this file keeps is the toll the metal pays to become continental. The Door and What It Admits The four ports of the Basin each admit one thing, and Dzong-Tamu admits the metal. Iron, steel, copper, and the ritually-restricted gold come down from the Ngaru-Bon highland and enter circulation here, and the entry is a…

The four predecessor ruin-sites named below are not haunted; they are bookable. Imajīn caravan-mistresses' factor-correspondence files them under the same operational category as oasis-cisterns and rubāṭ-fort waystations — load-bearing infrastructure whose habitability is bureaucratically maintained. The maintenance is paid out of the Imajīn Caravan Council's dust-tithe pool on a recurrent line-item basis; the foggara cleaning is contracted out to the ghūlām-manumission cohort whose post-manumission Ḥarrāb-class status keeps them in the Council's commercial orbit; the per-site safe-haven status is adjudicated by the Qalībin water-court at ʕAyn-Ṣalqat on a biennial review cycle. None of the discipline is romantic. The discipline of this file is to keep that tone. The ɣīlān-refuge mechanic that makes these sites continental waypoints — rather than archaeological curiosities the Imajīn would be free to bypass — is geographic engineering against a documented territorial pattern, not ancient wards or demonic exclusion zones. Practitioners hold that the predecessor's stone-cool assembly chambers were laid with a placement-discipline that produces shelter against ɣīlān whose…

Reading Discipline Ghadam-Thalla is the westernmost oasis of the Irrah confederation, a border town and a chokepoint, and the discipline of this file is to describe a place defined by two things it controls and one thing beneath it that it can no longer control at all. It controls the corridor up to the Ngaru-Bon plateau, through which the confederation's iron arrives; it controls the western anchor of the Spine, the central trunk road, and a leg of the Southern Thread toward the Ndjadi delta; and beneath it, on the descending escarpment, lies a Garamantes-shadow refuge-site whose safe-passage certification has lapsed and which the institutions above are about to vote on abandoning. The prose stays in the register of the dust-tithe ledger and the certification-filing — who pays for the reroute, who will not, which guild names the lapsed chamber and which refuses to — and not in the register of the frontier romance. The town's name describes its position exactly. Ghadam, the lower slope; thalla, the running spring water: the Foothill of the Running-Water, an oasis perched above the descending escarpment where the desert breaks toward the Ngaru-Bon highlands and the spring runs…

Reading Discipline Halani-Tamu is the east-shore port of the Aethelian Basin and the place where the sea-trade becomes the land-trade, and this file keeps the register of the tithe-booth and the route-certificate, not the spectacle of the widest crowd on the continent outside Tavakh-Qarat. The dockside is Oravan and the landside is Irrah and the bazaar between them is pure Basin chaos, and all of that is the texture; the subject is that this is the one door at which a cargo changes not hands only but element — comes off the water onto the camel-road, or off the road onto the water — and that the changing is taxed twice and certified once. Where the queen-church's weather-knowledge ends and the path-finders' desert-knowledge belongs to their own families and registers; this file follows the cargo across the seam, and the tithe it pays to cross. The Door and What It Admits The four ports of the Basin each admit one thing, and Halani-Tamu admits the switch — it is the continent's only joint between maritime and terrestrial trade, the point at which the Oravan sea-lanes hand their cargo to the Irrah overland routes and take the inland goods back to the water. The dhows come in to…

Reading Discipline Halkar Straits is the narrow passage at the mouth of the Aethelian Basin, the gate between the enclosed sea and the open ocean, and the discipline of this file is to describe it as a toll-gate held by a navy — a strait whose every transit is piloted, fee'd, and rated by the Oravan, and whose width is small enough that the holding is absolute. The prose stays in the register of the harbor-fee schedule and the pilot's book: how wide the strait runs at its narrowest, what passes through it and how often, whose pilot-houses and whose rates govern the passage, where the books are settled and in what season, and what becomes of a captain who declines the pilot. It does not reach for the register of the sea-passage sublime, the narrows-and-the-open-water of the mariner's tale. The strait is a real strait and a real drowner of the unpiloted, and it is also a length of water whose tolls underwrite a thalassocracy and whose refusal has cost three captains their return, and the second set of facts is the one the pilot-houses keep. The strait carries the name of the Oravan capital that commands it. Halkar is canonically the Oravan political and religious center — Hala…

Reading Discipline Hassag-Nganin is where the Ndjadi delta's five distributaries braid before the sea, and the discipline of this file is to describe the braid as hydrology and point to the theology, not to retell it. The five channels are a physical fact — they carry silt, split and rejoin, and have done so since before either the Ndjadi or the Irrah named them — and the cosmological significance attached to them is the religion file's territory. What this file keeps is the register of the water: how the distributaries meet, what the meeting does to navigation and sediment and the grain-trade that passes through Ki-Mbuhari downstream, and how the hydrology serves as the fixed anchor for a dispute that plays out entirely in manuscript. The water-covenant contestation — whether the five are the Ndjadi triad plus two unnamed waters or the Irrah Five Waters in a different guise — belongs to and is cross-referenced here, not duplicated. The Delta and What It Braids The Ndjadi delta spreads across the Basin's south shore in a five-mouth fan, and Hassag-Nganin is the point where the five mouths are still braided together — not yet separated into distinct channels, not yet merged into…

Reading Discipline Kalli-Xal is a single-clan Kheshkai caravanserai on the Breath-of-Cloud crossing, east of Tepet-Apu on Leg 2 of the Highland-Steppe Corridor, and its structural function is rations-only resupply: grain-pits and corralled mounts kept under a single clan-lord's seal, where travelers take on food before the run to the truce-site and beyond. It is not a waystation in the full sense — no water beyond what travelers carry, no neutral ground, no oath-bound truce — but a relay point in the Kheshkai steppe's own network, the last place a traveler is under single-clan authority before entering the mixed jurisdiction of Tepet-Apu. What this file keeps is the register of the relay: how the grain-pits are stocked, how the grazing toll is settled, and how the caravanserai's single-clan jurisdiction differs from the dual jurisdiction of the truce-site to its west. The Sand-House and What It Relays Kalli-Xal sits on a slight rise in the steppe grassland, where the soil is sandy enough to make grain-storage practical — the pits can be dug without hitting the clay layer that holds water and rots grain — and the rise is visible from a distance, a landmark in a landscape that…

Reading Discipline Kelata-Tamu is the outer Kelata sister-island in the Oravan archipelago, a freshwater waystation on the Coastal Monsoon route where a spring chambered into lava rock provides the sweetwater that ships need before they run the Halkar Straits into the Basin. Its structural function is simple and essential: it is the last Oravan-side source of reliable freshwater before the open Basin crossing, and vessels that do not tank here must carry their water from Halkar, reducing cargo capacity and increasing risk. What this file keeps is the register of the spring and the slack-tide rule, not the pilgrim customs of the obsidian-trade circuit or the theology of the First Caldera route that passes through here. The water is the subject; the rites are mentioned only as they affect access. The Sister-Island and What It Holds Kelata is the primary obsidian harvesting and export center of the Oravan archipelago — the port where the volcanic glass is quarried, knapped, and loaded for continental shipment. Kelata-Tamu is its smaller sister-island, separated by a narrow channel that runs fast at flood and ebb and calms at slack tide. What the sister-island holds is a freshwater…

Reading Discipline Khulūt is the southern incense city of the Irrah confederation, the oasis where the desert's frankincense meets the delta's grain, and the discipline of this file is to describe it as a place that lives by two trades running in opposite directions through it and by the standing foreign institution that the more powerful of those trades has planted in it. The prose stays in the register of the contract and the consular filing — what grade of incense is graded and by whom, where the grain is received and on whose account, which disputes the embassy's water-court subsection hears and under whose jurisdiction it sits, which descent-station below the town is certified and what the delta calls it. It does not reach for the register of the incense-route reverie. Khulūt is a southern customs-and-consular town, and the perfume of it is also a graded, taxed, contracted commodity that two civilizations have agreed how to weigh. The name is the strangest of the oasis chain and the most exact. The root √kh-l-w carries the sense of being empty, of passing through, of the interval between two filled things — Khulūt, "The Intervals" — and it names the town's position…

Reading Discipline Ki-Mbuhari is the south-shore port of the Aethelian Basin, the door by which the Ndjadi floodplain's grain enters the continent's circulation, and this file describes the door and the toll that books it, not the city's texture for its own sake. Every cross-civilizational legal question is a negotiation among the contributing civilizations' internal authorities, mediated by commercial institutions whose doctrinal status is "coordination" and whose practical effect is "sanction." The file documents the architecture of that negotiation: the institutions that pretend to adjudicate, the institutions that actually enforce, the seams where jurisdiction fails, and the crisis-legal deadlocks that result. Three load-bearing constraints govern the entire layer: 1. The Triple-Seal Arbitration Court is a Basin institution, not a continental one. Its jurisdiction is limited to contracts sealed at Basin port-zone venues. Etymology: var (oath, promise) + kosh (wind). "Oath-wind" — the sacred register of the Kheshkai steppe-peoples. Phonological Character Alone among the six, Varkosh has no institution. There are no colleges, no guilds, no lineages in the formal sense. Master-shamans take one to three apprentices; apprenticeship runs five to ten years on horseback during seasonal migration. Identification is by "hearing-gift" — a phonological capacity often associated with perfect-pitch individuals — detectable in children aged eight to twelve. The phonology is strict: - Back-vowel harmony in /a, o/ governs binding oaths, investiture, and war. The canonical pattern is a-o-a, preserved in the name Qarughan and transmitted through the Qarughan investiture-cycle. - Front-vowel harmony in /i/ governs domestic blessings, horse-consecrations, and well-namings. - Broken harmony is unmarked everyday speech — non-binding. - Harmonic completeness is absolute: a single disharmonic syllable voids the utterance. - Rising terminal intonation and glottal-onset emphatic stress are characteristic; the register is designed to project upward, under open sky. Phonological Character Gyamsgra's defining feature is the three-tier ancestral sub-register structure: - Nokul-tier with dental click [ǀ] — cattle-origin blessings - Amori-tier with lateral click [ǁ] — inventory and resource-counting - Lapam-tier with lateral fricative [ɬ] — metal consecration and weapon-genealogy The shift from click to non-click encodes, in the phonology itself, the civilizational transition from pastoral to industrial — a compression of historical narrative into articulatory gesture. Etymology: tava (voice) + mala (craft). "Craft-voice" — the sacred register of the Oravan palace-priestesshood. Phonological Character Vernacular Oravan is a non-tonal, open-syllable language whose vowel-length distinction is allophonic. In Tavamala, the distinction becomes phonemic and obligatorily carries a high-falling [˥˩] contour on lengthened vowels. Ritual reduplication — taa-ma taa-ma with sacred lengthening, against the vernacular emphatic tama tama — produces a characteristic sing-song recognizable across a harbor. Etymology: willka (sacred, sun-related) + qallu (throat, passage, from kullku). "Sacred tongue" — the calendrically-gated register of the Qollari. This phonological distinction carries theological weight -- the guild's internal hierarchy is encoded in articulatory position. The pharyngeal coda -ʕa in the liturgical form is the most difficult element for non-native speakers. Combined with the lateral click onset, the full form requires two independent articulatory feats that mark the speaker as guild-trained from infancy. The common-use form Amori retains only the vowel skeleton (a-o-i), making it accessible to Basin merchants and foreign partners. In-World Gloss > "Amori counts at dusk. He counts again at dawn. He counts you twice." This phrase is spoken at cattle-counts and…

The Ndjadi ka-tier mortal-ordered entity. Juridical, market-facing, the principle of measurement and exchange. The ka- prefix marks the structured, human-scale cosmological tier. Name and Etymology Kagbende -- common-use form. Sacred-register form: Ka-Gbénde (prefix ka- + labial-velar root -gbé- "to measure/weigh" + nominalizer -nde; juridical tone-contour in liturgical pronunciation). The ka- prefix marks the mortal-ordered tier -- the domain of structured human activity, law, commerce, and correct proportion. Unlike the ra- primordial tier (uncreated, ground-of-being) and the nga- chthonic tier (underground, localized), ka- marks what is built, maintained, and adjudicated by human effort operating within cosmological structure. The labial-velar gb- onset is characteristic of Ndjadi's heavier consonant inventory. In ordinary speech, kagbende names a market-weight standard. In liturgical speech, the prefix separates and the juridical tone-contour activates: Ka-Gbénde, marking the utterance as a cosmological claim about the nature of fair measure. In-World Gloss > "Ka-Gbénde walks the market at dawn; the scales tilt when he turns his head." This phrase is spoken by…

The Qollari Sky figure. The Sky read as impersonal LAW -- calendrical order whose correct measurement licenses corridor access. Not a person who judges but a pattern that either aligns or does not. Name and Etymology Karuwel -- common-use form. Sacred-register form preserves the ejective origin: Q'aruwél (ejective uvular q'- + root -aru- "vertical/above" + theonymic coda -wél; the rare glide-coda appears only in deity-class names in Qollari). The ejective uvular q' is characteristic of Qollari sacred register -- consonants that require precise articulatory force, bound to specific calendrical days. In ordinary speech, karuwel drops the ejective (the common-use form simplifies the onset to plain k-), making the name accessible to non-practitioners. The liturgical form with ejective onset is reserved for solstitial and equinoctial rites. The q ↔ q' correspondence between Kheshkai Qarughan and Qollari Karuwel (underlying Q'aruwel) is regular across the Sky Witness cognate layer. Kheshkai loses the ejective (no ejectives in inventory) and replaces the -wél coda with native participial -ğan. Both forms derive from a shared proto-concept. The Ngaru-Bon forge-ancestor. The industrial transition figure -- "works behind the wall the cattle cannot pass." Third in the Ngaru-Bon ancestral sequence, marking the shift from pastoral to metallurgical civilization. Name and Etymology Lapam -- common-use form. Sacred-register form: Ɬap'ami (lateral fricative ɬ- + ejective root -ap'- "to strike hot" + ancestor-suffix -ami). The critical phonological feature: Lapam's liturgical form deliberately lacks a click. Both Nokul (ǀ- dental click) and Amori (ǁ- lateral click) are click-initial. Lapam's lateral fricative ɬ- onset is a categorically different sound -- airstream mechanism shifted from velaric (click) to pulmonic (fricative). Practitioners explain this as marking the industrial-ancestor tier: clicks belong to the cattle-era ancestors, the lateral fricative belongs to the forge-era. The phonological boundary IS the civilizational transition. The ejective -p'- in the root "to strike hot" is produced by glottalic airstream -- a third airstream mechanism in one name (pulmonic, glottalic). The phonological complexity marks Lapam as the most technically demanding figure to invoke in full liturgical form, which guild…

The Oravan dyadic figure. Two aspects, not two gods. The ocean and the hearth are the same hand. Name and Etymology Maawara -- base mawara "salt-mother-water" with sacred vowel-length on root. Two aspect-epithets: - Maawara Taasi (ocean aspect) -- taasi "long salt" - Maawara Apii (hearth aspect) -- apii "inner flame"; never reduplicated (reduplication would demote to household-familiar status) The sacred vowel-length (maa- rather than ma-) is the register-mark. In ordinary speech, mawara means simply "salt-water." The lengthened form enters the sacred register of Oravan artisan-priests. This is an innovative feature, not inherited -- the Qalībin's counter-argument against cognacy with Ndjadi Ramwen rests partly on this point. In-World Gloss > "She who salts the bowl and lights the bowl. Same hand." This is the foundational liturgical phrase, spoken at every workshop initiation. It encodes the dual-aspect doctrine: salt (ocean) and fire (hearth/volcanic) are not opposites balanced against each other but the same creative-destructive force expressed in two media. Islands are born from fire and salt simultaneously; fleets are destroyed by the same combination. Theological…

The Ndjadi nga-tier chthonic entity. River-bends, underground waters, the places where flow forgets its direction. The nga- prefix marks the localized, earthbound, subterranean cosmological tier. Name and Etymology Ngandim -- common-use form. Sacred-register form: Nga-Ndímba (prefix nga- + prenasalized root -ndím- "to coil/river-bend" + class marker -ba; breathy medial vowel in liturgical pronunciation). The nga- prefix marks the chthonic tier -- underground, localized, site-specific. Where ra- (Ramwen) names the uncreated source and ka- (Kagbende) names the mortal-ordered structure, nga- names what has sunk below, coiled back, or become bound to a specific place. The prefix is the same one used for localized spirits (nga-beli) in everyday Ndjadi, which creates a deliberate taxonomic ambiguity: is Ngandim a deity or the largest spirit? Scribal colleges disagree. The prenasalized cluster nd- plus the breathy medial in liturgical form make this the most phonologically marked of the three tier-figures in sacred-register speech. Ordinary pronunciation (ngandim) drops the breathy quality and the class suffix, collapsing the liturgical complexity into a manageable proper noun.…

The Ngaru-Bon first-ancestor. Cattle-origin figure -- "struck the first hollow" that cattle answered. The founding act of Ngaru-Bon civilization is an acoustic event: a hollow struck, an animal responding before a person could. Name and Etymology Nokul -- common-use form. Sacred-register form: ǀNoɬa (dental click ǀ- + root -noɬ- "to stretch a skin/to hollow" + class marker -a; the click IS the name in liturgical speech). The radical simplification from ǀNoɬa to Nokul demonstrates the sacred-register concept perfectly: the liturgical form requires a dental click and lateral fricative that non-Ngaru-Bon speakers cannot produce. The common-use form strips these to accessible consonants (n-, -k-, -l), making the name speakable across the continent. Ngaru-Bon practitioners consider the common form a convenience, not the real name -- "you say Nokul; we say what he is." The dental click ǀ- in the liturgical form is the most significant phoneme. Clicks enter Ngaru-Bon infants through parental speech from birth; the acquisition window closes in early childhood. An adult learner can approximate but never achieve the articulatory precision required for sacred-register use. This is not…

The Oravan Fire-House figure. The fire at the center of the house, the roof-beam junction, the domestic hearth. Not Maawara's hearth-aspect -- a separate, older entity. Name and Etymology Pulino -- common-use form. Sacred-register form: Pulinaa (puli "pillar-wood" + agentive -na + sacred length -aa). The sacred length -aa marks the register boundary. In ordinary speech, pulino names the central roof-beam junction of a traditional Oravan house. The lengthened liturgical form Pulinaa enters artisan-priest speech only during construction rites and hearth-lighting. Reduplication is forbidden. Where Oravan sacred register typically intensifies through reduplication (e.g., tama tama → taa-ma taa-ma), Pulino resists this pattern. Workshop-lineages explain this differently -- some say reduplication would "spread the fire beyond the house" (catastrophe), others that Pulino is too old for the reduplication system (pre-Water-Covenant claim). The prohibition itself is universal across all workshop-lineages even where the explanation diverges. In-World Gloss > "Pulino stands where the four roof-beams meet. Do not set the pot on her." This phrase is spoken during hearth-lighting ceremonies.…

The Kheshkai Sky figure. The ONE named high entity in Kheshkai theology. Not a god who blesses or curses -- a presence that notes. The Sky as impersonal WILL read through shamanistic interpretation. Name and Etymology Qarughan -- common-use form. Sacred-register form: Qaruğan (back-harmony root qar- "that-which-watches-from-above" + -uğ- abstract-elevation suffix + participial -an; uvular q + velar-fricative ğ in liturgical pronunciation). The back-harmony vowel pattern (a-o-a) is characteristic of Kheshkai sacred speech. The language's vowel-harmony system -- where an oath in perfect harmony binds and a broken-harmony oath is a non-oath -- makes the phonological form itself load-bearing. Qarughan's name is, in this sense, already a correctly-formed utterance: the harmonious back-vowel chain enacts the binding it names. In ordinary steppe speech, qarughan serves as an impersonal construction: "it is noted," "it is watched." The participial -an ending gives it the quality of ongoing observation rather than completed act. The sky is always noting. For Kheshkai speakers, this is not metaphor -- it is a literal description of how the Sky works. In-World Gloss > "Qarughan does not…

The Qollari Ancestor-Stone figure. Mountain-facing, genealogical. The ancestor who became stone, whose back is every road. Reflects Qollari's membership in the Ancestor-Stone complex alongside their Sky-Mandate membership. Name and Etymology Qullpar -- common-use form. Sacred-register form: Qhullpar (aspirated uvular qh- + root -ull- "set-in-place/weighted" + agentive -par; geminate -ll- + stop cluster tolerated only for ancestor-class names in Qollari phonotactics). The aspirated uvular qh- distinguishes ancestor-class names from sky-class names (which use ejective q'-). This phonological distinction IS a theological one: ejective onset = sky-tier, aspirated onset = stone-tier. The common-use form Qullpar neutralizes the aspiration, making the name accessible outside liturgical contexts. The geminate -ll- plus stop cluster (-llp-) is phonotactically heavy -- permitted only in ancestor-class proper nouns. Ordinary Qollari words avoid this combination. The weight of the consonant cluster is (practitioners say) iconic: the name is heavy because the ancestor is heavy. Stone names sound like stone. In-World Gloss > "Qullpar's face is turned into the mountain. His back is every…

The Ndjadi ra-tier primordial entity. Not a person in the Oravan sense -- a grammaticalized cosmological position. The ra- prefix IS the theological claim. Name and Etymology Ramwen -- common-use form. Sacred-register form: Ra-Mwéne (prefix ra- + prenasalized root -mwén- "to open/source" + class marker -e; high-tone penult in liturgical pronunciation). The ra- prefix marks the primordial cosmological tier in Ndjadi grammatical theology. Three tiers exist: - ra- -- primordial, uncreated, ground-of-being - ka- -- mortal-ordered, structured, juridical - nga- -- chthonic, underground, localized Ramwen occupies the highest tier. In ordinary Ndjadi speech, ramwen functions as a proper noun without active prefix analysis. In liturgical speech, the prefix is stressed and separated: Ra-Mwéne, foregrounding the cosmological claim. Scribal-priests who use the wrong tier-prefix for this figure are not making a grammar error -- they are making a theological error with (practitioners say) cosmological consequences. In-World Gloss > "Ra-Mwéne opens her mouth at the delta; her teeth are the sandbars." This liturgical phrase is spoken during delta-mouth rites at the seasonal flood's arrival.…

Irrah ancestor figure. Explicitly NOT a deity -- classified as ancestor by Qalībin, keeping Irrah's structural rule: no named high deity. The Great Sealer, who stamps the tomb-brick. The highest-ranked named figure in Irrah, and still only an ancestor. Name and Etymology Tabbaq -- common-use form. Sacred-register form: Ṭabbāʕ (√ṭ-b-ʕ "to stamp/to impress a seal" in intensive-agent pattern CaC₁C₁āC₂ → "the Great Stamper/Sealer"). The triconsonantal root system is characteristic of Irrah's Qalib sacred register. The intensive-agent pattern (CaC₁C₁āC₂) doubles the middle radical and lengthens the final vowel, marking the form as denoting someone who performs the action professionally and intensively -- not someone who once stamped, but "the one whose nature is stamping." The common-use form Tabbaq simplifies the emphatic ṭ- to plain t- and the pharyngeal coda -ʕ to plain -q (uvular stop substituted for the pharyngeal fricative -- a regular simplification in Basin trade speech). The full liturgical form requires the emphatic and pharyngeal articulations that mark trained Qalib speakers. The root √ṭ-b-ʕ belongs to the oath-binder profession's phonotactic subset.
