Disposal: Desert burial in raised tower-tombs and cairns, strung into funerary avenues that link oases and cluster at permanent water sources. The Rite In the Irrah drylands the dead are buried in stone chambers raised above the sand, shaped from the same rock that holds the wells. A body is washed, wrapped, and placed in the chamber with its face turned toward the route its lineage traveled, and the chamber is sealed under a tower-tomb or a low cairn depending on wealth and rank. The tombs are not scattered. They line the caravan avenues that run between oases, so that a traveler moving from well to well passes through corridors of the dead. The densest tombs stand at the permanent water sources, where several avenues meet and where the living must still pause to drink. Mourning is brief at the grave but renewed at each caravan season, when offerings are left at the avenue tombs before a major journey. Afterlife and Ancestors Irrah belief holds that the dead remain connected to the Five Waters, especially the hidden Tenth Water that once moved in their bodies. In the Five-Waters necropolis cult, the ancestors buried along an avenue are understood to keep the route open and the…

Disposal: Barrow burial under a raised earthen mound on the open steppe, accompanied by sacrificed horses, portable grave-goods, and, for the highest elite, a buried retinue. The Rite A Kheshkai death on the steppe interrupts the seasonal movement of the clan. The body is prepared, dressed in its best wool and gold, and placed in a wooden chamber dug into a chosen rise while kin drive horses and cattle to the site. Horses are sacrificed at the barrow's edge, their bones arranged so that the dead may ride, and the chamber is sealed beneath a mound of turf and stone that will stand long after the tents have moved on. The funeral lasts until the mound is complete, sometimes many days for a great khan, and ends with a feast and the swearing of oaths at the barrow's foot. For common clanspeople the mound is smaller, the goods fewer, and the rites shorter, but the shape is the same: a fixed mark made by a mobile people. Afterlife and Ancestors Kheshkai belief holds that the sky receives the worthy dead. The barrow is not a grave in the lowland sense but a launching place: the dead lord lies with his horses, his weapons, and his people, ready to enter the sky-order that Qarughan…

Disposal: Secondary processing in a charnel structure, followed by interment in or beneath a communal earthwork mound on the floodplain. The Rite When an Ndjadi householder dies, the body is first laid in a charnel house near the lineage compound while kin gather and the scribes begin the mourning record. After a period that may last from several weeks to a full season, the remains are gathered, sometimes bundled with selected bones of earlier dead from the same house, and placed within or beneath the lineage mound. The mound itself is not a single grave but a layered monument: each new burial adds earth, and the height and width of a mound record the accumulated deaths and labor of a kin-group. Mourning continues through planting and harvest rites, when the dead are addressed as part of the river-order that governs the delta. Afterlife and Ancestors Ndjadi belief holds that the dead do not leave the river-order. They sink into the same earth the river renews each flood, and from that earth they continue to anchor their kin-group in the cosmic grammar of the Water-Covenant. The mound is understood as a vertical charnel-house, with older dead deeper and newer dead higher, each…

Disposal: Two registers governed by plateau scarcity: excarnation and sky-exposure for most, and rock-hewn burial inside a sacred monumental complex for the elite. The Rite On the high plateau wood is too scarce to burn a body and the ground is too hard to dig graves for everyone, so the dead of ordinary households are carried to an exposed stone platform and laid out for the air and the birds. The flesh is removed from the world in the natural order of height, and the bones are gathered afterward for placement in a cairn or a niche. For kings, great smith-lords, and the founders of guild-lines, the body is instead carried into the rock-church complex and interred in a hewn chamber within the consecrated stone. The difference is not only rank but access to metal: the elite burial requires tools, labor, and guild authorization that common households cannot command. Mourning lasts until the commemorative feast is held, sometimes a year after death, when the land-grant that funds it is publicly confirmed. Afterlife and Ancestors Ngaru-Bon belief holds that the ancestor is literally in the worked material. For the sky-exposed dead, the bones return to the stone of the plateau; for…

Disposal: Collective burial in a shared lineage tomb, with secondary treatment of bones and a maritime strand in which the dead are sent toward the sea. The Rite When an Oravan householder dies, the body is first laid on a stone shelf in the lineage tomb while kin bring oil, wine, and the first fruits appropriate to the season. After the flesh has gone, the bones are gathered, and selected skulls and long bones are arranged in clay chests or niches along the tomb walls. The tomb itself is reused across generations, sometimes for centuries, so that a single chamber holds the dead of a whole lineage. For those who die at sea, the body is committed to the water from a boat, and a small clay token bearing the lineage mark is placed in the tomb instead. Mourning is marked by recurring gatherings at the tomb, not by a single funeral, and the largest gatherings coincide with the calmer sailing seasons when many kin are ashore. Afterlife and Ancestors Oravan belief holds that the dead remain present in the lineage tomb and that the sea carries what must travel. Each of the six civilizations does something different with its dead, and each does it for reasons that cannot be settled. This layer documents disposal, mourning, the funerary economy, and who officiates, across all six. It does not settle whether the dead persist. That question is held open on purpose. The Undecidable Dead The reality of the afterlife is permanently undecidable in Veydria, exactly as the sacred registers are (see and ADR-0026). No funerary practice confirms that the dead hear, own, or answer, and none confirms that they are simply gone. Every per-civ file therefore carries two readings that the data layer never adjudicates: - a practitioner's reading, in which the dead persist and must be served, kept, or consulted, and the rite does real work; - a skeptic's reading, in which the practice is doing inheritance, succession, social memory, and legitimacy work, materially and without remainder. This is the four-layer ambiguity of (Design Rail 2, no confirmed deities; Rail 7, ambiguity preserved) extended to mortality. The practitioner's reading is carried by the believers in the file; the skeptic's reading is carried by the naturalists every Veydrian tradition…

Disposal: Highland cold desiccation, wrapping, and curation; the dead lineage-head remains a present social person rather than an interred memory. The Rite The Qollari highlands do not favor decay. Cold, dry air above the terraced valleys draws moisture from a corpse faster than burial would hide it, so the body is cleaned, desiccated, wrapped in dyed cloth, and seated in a dry niche within the lineage house or a small ancestral chamber. The wrapping is not a farewell but a preparation: the dead continue to sit at council, to receive offerings, and to be addressed on matters of land and succession. Mourning lasts through one full agricultural cycle, during which the household suspends major decisions until the preserved head has been formally consulted. A younger heir may be invested with office before the cycle ends, but the property itself remains spoken of as belonging to the seated dead. Afterlife and Ancestors Qollari belief holds that the dead do not depart. A preserved lineage-head is tended as one who still hears, still owns, and still answers through the intermediaries who keep him. This is the Ancestor-Stone principle made literal in flesh: the ancestor is a fixed…

The Aethelian Basin has no calendar. This is not an absence. It is an architecture. Where other civilizations declare time — the Qollari priesthood through khipu intercalation, the Oravan priestess-queen through solstice consecration, the Irrah scholar through isnād-certified star-reading — the Basin receives time. Four ports host six foreign calendars and compose from their overlap a commercial rhythm that no single civilization authored and none can unilaterally amend. The Basin's temporal authority is procedural, not declarative. It does not ask which calendar is correct. It asks which contract was sealed with the seven-stroke Filer's Hand before witnesses who remained for the full cadence. The Composite Year The Basin does not count years. It counts rotations. A Basin "year" is the complete circuit of the Triple-Seal Arbitration Court through four port zones — Tavakh-Qarat, Ki-Mbuhari, Halani-Tamu, Dzong-Tamu — each hosted at the season when that port's ecological and administrative conditions are most stable. The Court packs its seals, its witness-rosters, and its senior arbitrators' personal familiarity with each port's variant of the Filer's Hand, and moves. A…

A loose fraternity of skeptical scholars concentrated in Aethelian port cities. Not an institution in the strict sense -- no hierarchy, no initiation, no buildings. A network of people who share a specific intellectual position: the sacred registers work, but calling their effects "divine" is a category error. Tamah bint Sarqaf The founder-figure. Her treatise On the Breath of Stones (c. 80 years before the playable present) argues: 1. Ghilan are observable ecological entities -- marsh-lights, cave pressure-anomalies, canyon acoustic echoes -- without moral stance toward humans 2. Sacred-register magic produces real, costly, ambiguous effects explicable as learned acoustic-psychological engineering 3. Therefore, calling these phenomena "divine" is a category error Tamah does not deny the sacred register works. She denies its theological interpretation. This is closer to Xenophanes and Carvaka than to modern atheism. She is not saying "there are no gods." She is saying "what you call gods are natural phenomena that we happen to interact with through trained phonological performance." Tamah herself was, per surviving accounts, personally vindictive and professionally corrupt. Her…

The Irrah year is not declared. It is certified. Twelve months indexed to Azmarāʔ star-readings exist in parallel across the oasis-courts, each computation independently derived, each valid if its scholar's isnād-chain is unbroken. There is no single calendar. There are many calendars, and their agreement is institutionally normal. This distributed architecture is the deep inversion of Qollari. Where Qollari has one declared system whose schism is catastrophic because everyone is on it, Irrah has many certified systems whose divergence is the default state. A caravan-master who departs on the date certified by one Azmarāʔ scholar and arrives at a Basin port where another scholar's computation prevails does not experience a crisis. He experiences the ordinary texture of Irrah time. The Azmarāʔ Star-Readings as Year Anchor The year's master rhythm is solar-astronomical, computed from star-positions observed at each oasis-court venue. The Azmarāʔ sub-register — the Qalībin path-finders who own the glottalic and uvural phonological monopoly — transmits the computation methodology through isnād-chains that connect every certifying scholar back through named teachers to the…

The Kheshkai do not have a calendar. This is not an absence. It is a doctrine. "Basin calendars are paper and paper does not know the grass." The Oral-Memory Council's senior speaker delivered this ruling six master-shaman transmission cycles ago, in response to a Khazadari clerk who proposed that the Council's pasture-rotation hearings be transcribed into Basin contract notation. The ruling stands. The Council has refused every subsequent proposal for written codification — from Tongue-Guild basin-port translators, from Ndjadi scribal reformers, from Qollari khipu-record keepers who argued that the Three-Year Skyward required a shared temporal notation. This file documents the refusal. It is not a calendar in the Qollari or Ndjadi sense. It is an account of how a civilization keeps time without keeping records. The Oral-Memory Council The Aman-Sanah Zövlöl is the only authoritative record of Kheshkai time. Its membership is not fixed. Any clan elder who has witnessed three pasture-rotation hearings may speak. Any master-shaman who has completed a transmission cycle may challenge a ruling. The Council convenes at the autumn festival circuit, at the spring thaw campaign…

Legitimize but cannot constrain. Their confederation-consensus structure means when a khan wins, the argument ends; when he loses, shamans switch sides. They set up no permanent institutions. They travel with caravans, witness on the move, collect fees, vanish. How They Work Sky-shamans diagnose Qarughan's will retroactively. They do not predict outcomes -- they interpret them after the fact. A khan wins a battle; the shaman confirms the sky approved. A khan's horse dies on the morning of a raid; the shaman advises retreat. The diagnosis is always post-hoc, which makes it unfalsifiable and structurally honest: the shaman never promises what the sky will do, only reads what it meant. The shaman is identified by "hearing-gift" -- often individuals with perfect pitch or exceptional sensitivity to harmonic patterns. Training is master-to-apprentice on horseback, oral-only, with no scribal tradition. Every generation re-negotiates orthodoxy because there is no text to anchor it. A shaman's authority is personal and contingent, not institutional. The Ndjadi year is not a circle. It is a pulse — a single annual flood that rises, crests, recedes, and leaves the land either sown or hungry. There is no spring, no summer, no autumn, no winter. There is only the flood, the recession, the growing, and the hungry gap. The calendar is hydrology, not astronomy. The Flood as Year Anchor The year begins when the Floodwatch Augmented Bureaucracy publishes the flood-window prediction. This is not a celebration. It is a ruling. The prediction classifies the coming year as "ordinary," "heavy," or "low" flood, and that classification determines the levy schedule, the harvest-guarantee underwriting terms, and the volume of prefix-notarization the Court of the Three Mouths will process. The prediction is based on gauge-readings from a network of upstream stations whose data is compiled by the Floodwatch and ratified at the River-Lord House Assembly convened the week after publication. The Assembly elects a rotating speaker; the Floodwatch does not vote. The classification is technically determined and not subject to commercial override — though three upstream irrigation districts have disputed the "ordinary" designation for the current…

The people who certify correct speech. Since correct speech IS prayer, the scribes who control certification hold a functional veto over any public act that requires liturgical authorization. They are notaries, priests, and cosmological regulators in one institution. The Grammatical Mechanism Ndjadi sacred grammar maps a three-tier cosmological order onto every noun through prefixes: - ra- -- primordial tier (the oldest, most fundamental things: the delta itself, the original water, the foundational concepts) - ka- -- mortal-ordered tier (human institutions, tools, settlements, everything made by living people) - nga- -- chthonic tier (underground, ancestral, spirit-level entities) A misapplied prefix is not a grammar error. It is a cosmological miscategorization with consequences. The canonical teaching-case parallels the Vedic indrashatru accent disaster: a word intended to mean one thing means its opposite when the accent (or in Ndjadi's case, the prefix) falls wrong. Calling a primordial entity by the chthonic prefix doesn't merely insult it -- it reclassifies it, and the reclassification persists. This is the strongest Veydria-specific invention in the whole religion…

The Ngaru-Bon year has two scales. The short scale — what merchants and farmers use — is a solar year of twelve months, anchored to the msasa red leaf-flush and the cool-dry-winter smelting-season opening. The long scale — what matters — is counted in ancestor-smith tier promotions: Nokul, Amori, Lapam. A generation is not a span of time. It is a name that may refer to one mortal, a sequence of inheritors, or a fiction the Outside-Forge Network maintains for institutional continuity. Neither the Inner Council nor outsiders can determine which without disrupting the institutional position. The Smelting Season as Year Anchor The year's most important transition is not the sowing, though the msasa's red leaf-flush signals it. The year's most important transition is the opening of the cool-dry-winter smelting season, when the bloomeries relight and iron is made. This is when the continent's steel supply is determined. The Inner Council's consecration schedule gates the year's production. Each bloomery operation must be preceded by a reconsecration rite whose timing is set by the Council's ritual bell, click-register access, and forge-temple grain allocation. A bloom that fires…

Legitimize by constraint. The guild controls both ritual and military production. Their Investiture-Controversy-style interdict is a forge-strike -- refusing to produce weapons or reconsecrate tools. Great Zimbabwe's dzimbahwe logic: rainmaker kings depend on ancestor-sanctioned regalia that the guild makes. The Guild Structure The ancestor-smith guild is patrilineal and hereditary. Membership is by birth into a guild family, apprenticeship beginning in infancy. The guild is not a priesthood -- smiths are craftspeople whose craft happens to be sacred. The distinction matters: they do not preach, do not maintain temples, do not perform public rituals. They forge, and the forging IS the ritual. The guild controls: - Weapon production. Every blade, spearhead, and piece of armor on the plateau passes through guild forges. Unforged metal is not weaponry -- it is raw material. - Tool reconsecration. Agricultural and mining tools must be periodically reconsecrated through forge-chanting. The Oravan year is not computed. It is performed. The priestess-queen's body at the solstice Tavamala Consecration is the only instrument capable of opening the sailing year, and her physical absence — whether by death, dispute, or cyclone — closes it. There are no archivists, no knot-records, no star-tables. There is only the ocean-salt register on her left hand and the hearth-fire register on her right, and the declaration she makes when both are present. This makes the Oravan calendar the most fragile on the continent. A succession crisis is never merely political. It is a calendrical suspension during which convoys cannot sail insured, the Harbor Covenant's wave-tithe receipt-book cannot be stamped, and the Three-Cove Concord's parallel pricing circulars gain commercial force precisely because the official calendar has stopped. The Monsoon as Year Anchor The year's master rhythm is bimodal: the wet northwest monsoon brings convective rain and breadfruit fruiting through the lunar months the islanders call the "water quarter"; the drier southeast trade season opens the clove-nutmeg harvest and the canoe-voyaging window. Every succession dispute is simultaneously a theological one. This is the civ most vulnerable to schism-as-civil-war. The Fusion Model Oravan palace-priestesses operate on the Fifth Dalai Lama's Ganden Phodrang model (1642): spiritual and temporal authority collapse into one office. The priestess-queen does not rule by divine right -- she rules because the office IS the goddess in institutional form. When an Oravan priestess taxes a harbor, the tax IS the liturgy. There is no church-state separation because the distinction does not exist. The palace functions as the largest artisan-workshop. Artisan-priests work under the priestess-queen's authority, combining craft-production with sacred-register invocation. Every significant craft act is a ritual act. The Irrah water-scholar order. A quietist institution whose doctrinal restraint is precisely what makes it the richest and most geographically pervasive religious body on the continent. The Quietist Creed "Water does not serve one house." The foundational principle is structural, not merely pious. The Qalībin holds that the Five Waters -- surface, underground, sky, dew, and the Tenth Water (bodily/hidden) -- are cosmological categories that exist prior to civilization and cannot be owned, directed, or enlisted by any political authority. A water-scholar who places the order's resources at the service of a specific house, faction, or war has misunderstood the nature of water itself. This is a Veydrian analog of the Suwarian tradition (al-Hajj Salim Suwari's quietist precepts among the Soninke/Jakhanke/Juula/Dyula merchant-clerical diaspora) combined with the Sanusiyya zawiya network (Muhammad ibn Ali al-Sanusi's 146 lodges by c. 1900). The Qalībin is a scholarly order like the rabbinate or ulama, not a hierarchy with a capital. There is no Qalībin caliph. A vertical hierarchy that legitimizes and constrains in one move. Trade-corridor access IS calendrical access. The calendar-priesthood functions like the Delphic Oracle as inter-polis arbitrator: opacity is power. The Calendar as Genealogy The Qollari calendar is not merely an astronomical instrument. It is a genealogical record. Dead lineages become fixed points in the sky -- stars, constellations, eclipse-recurrence positions. The calendar's accuracy is simultaneously scientific achievement and ancestor-honoring. Correcting the calendar means revising the genealogical record. This is what makes calendar-reform scandals politically explosive. When rival calendar-keeper lineages dispute an intercalation (whether to add a corrective day to prevent drift), they are simultaneously disputing whose ancestors occupy which celestial positions. An intercalation error is both an astronomical mistake and an insult to specific dead lineages. Ejective-Calendrical Magic Qollari magic is calendrical: ejective consonants bind to specific days in a ritual calendar. Uvulars are reserved for solstitial rites. Oravan monsoon-reversal pilgrimage. The ritual calendar IS the sailing calendar. Route and Timing The circuit follows the biannual monsoon reversal. Outbound: northeast monsoon carries ships from Aethelian ports toward the archipelago. Return: southwest monsoon brings them back. The timing is non-negotiable -- miss the monsoon window and you wait six months or risk open-ocean sailing without wind-support. This means the pilgrimage is structurally identical to the trade cycle. Every merchant vessel making the monsoon crossing is potentially a pilgrim vessel. Every pilgrim vessel carries cargo. Summary Kheshkai shamans use vowel-harmony as a binding grammar: an oath in perfect harmony binds; a broken-harmony oath is a non-oath, hearable-but-ineffectual. The system is oral-only (no scribal class), master-to-apprentice on horseback, and identified by "hearing-gift" (often perfect-pitch individuals). Each generation renegotiates orthodoxy. Summary Mixed-heritage individuals are rare, politically freighted, and irreplaceable. A child of an Irrah caravan-mother and an Oravan dockworker raised in the Basin might acquire pharyngeals AND vowel-length natively. They can articulate phrases across registers; they cannot legitimate them, because they lack isnad and initiation. They are security concerns for multiple institutions and hired by everyone. The Acquisition Problem Sacred registers are phonologically gated -- each requires articulatory skills best acquired in childhood. The standard model assumes monocultural upbringing: one register per person, acquired through one training pipeline, legitimated by one institutional chain. Mixed-heritage individuals break this model by acquiring multiple phonological systems natively through exposure to multiple linguistic environments in early childhood. This is not supernatural -- it is the same process by which bilingual children acquire two languages' phonologies without accent in either. Summary Tavas-Kaj is the Aethelian Basin's trade pidgin -- structurally leveled to remove every marked phonological feature that constitutes a sacred register. No clicks, no pharyngeals, no ejectives, no vowel-harmony constraints, no length-distinctions, no cosmological prefixes. This is exactly why it is trade-useful and magically inert. Loanwords enter Tavas-Kaj stripped of precisely the features that made them sacred. Tavas-Kaj is not a sacred register. It is the anti-register -- the linguistic space where all sacred material becomes costume. Its inclusion in this directory is structural: understanding what Tavas-Kaj strips explains what each register's load-bearing features are. The three-tier prefix system maps onto three of the five channels; the remaining two are "unnamed" -- either primordial (pre-prefix, older than the grammar) or fallen (once-named, now forgotten). A partly-submerged stepped platform at the Aethelian Basin's dead center. The most physically contested sacred site on the continent. Currently Oravan-garrisoned with Ndjadi time-sharing access. The Site A monumental stepped structure -- platforms descending into tidal water, the lowest courses permanently submerged, the upper courses exposed at low tide. The construction predates both Oravan and Ndjadi ethnogenesis. Neither civilization built it. Both claim it. The architecture is ambiguous by accident of geology: tidal submersion has eroded lower inscription layers while preserving upper ones, and periodic earthquakes have exposed, re-buried, and re-exposed different courses over centuries. Both Ngaru-Bon and Qollari treat ancestors-in-worked-stone as the civilization's political spine. The material differs -- Ngaru-Bon works metal, Qollari works terrace-stone -- but the principle is the same: ancestors are present in the material they shaped, and the material legitimizes the living through continuity of craft. Ngaru-Bon: Ancestors in Metal For Ngaru-Bon, the forge is where ancestors speak. Lapam -- "the striker" -- is the forge-ancestor who taught the first smith. The named-lineage ancestors (Nokul, Amori) are the cattle-keeper and counter who gave the culture its economic foundation. All three are ancestor-class figures, not deities -- they were people who became politically load-bearing after death. The ancestor-smith guild controls both ritual and military production. A forge-strike -- refusing to produce weapons or reconsecrate tools -- is the institutional lever. This parallels Investiture Controversy mechanics: the smiths don't command armies, but armies can't fight without their products. A local intensification on the Water-Covenant substrate, not a separate tradition family. The Fire-House fuses volcanic fire with the oceanic Water theology to produce something no other descendant of the Water-Covenant has: a dual-aspect divinity whose two media (salt water and volcanic fire) are treated as the same creative-destructive force. Why It's Not a Separate Family The Fire-House does not have its own substrate, its own proto-theology, or its own independent history. It is what happens when the Water-Covenant lands on volcanic islands. The fire was added to the water, not substituted for it. Oravan purification rites, tiered cosmogony, and the Tenth-Water-in-the-body concept are all Water-Covenant features. The fire -- the caldera, the eruption, the hearth -- is the local addition. This distinction matters for cross-civ analysis. When Ndjadi grammarians argue with Oravan priestesses about the Water-Covenant substrate, the fire element is not part of the dispute. The Ndjadi don't contest fire; they contest whether personalizing the Water is a valid development or a corruption. The fire is simply not their problem. Two civilizations -- Kheshkai and Qollari -- share a proto-concept of the Sky as an impersonal mandating order. Each moved in opposite interpretive directions. The shared substrate is NOT a proto-Sky god in the Tengri mold ("Central Asia with serial numbers filed off"). It is a concept: the sky orders, and the ordering can be read. The Substrate The Sky-Mandate substrate holds that the sky imposes order on the world below. This order is readable -- through weather, through star-positions, through seasonal cycles -- and the reading confers legitimacy. Whoever reads the sky correctly has the right to act. Unlike the Water-Covenant, the Sky-Mandate substrate did not leave behind a rich ritual vocabulary or a cosmological taxonomy. What it left is simpler and harder to fake: a shared conviction that the sky's order is impersonal, that reading it is a skill, and that the reading legitimizes action. The disagreement between Kheshkai and Qollari is over what "reading" means. Two Descendants, Opposite Metaphysics Kheshkai: The Sky as WILL Kheshkai reads the sky as a near-person. Qarughan -- "that-which-watches-from-above" -- does not bless and does not curse. He notes. The sky's favor…

Site-specific spirits that predate all named traditions. Rivers, passes, specific trees, particular wells, a named wind that blows in a specific wadi in a specific season. Every tradition has variably absorbed or suppressed them. They are the Veydrian equivalent of Shinto kami surviving under Buddhism, or ovoo cairns surviving under Central Asian Islam. What the Sub-Stratum Is These are not gods, not ancestors, not cosmological categories. They are place-entities. A spirit of a specific spring. A presence at a specific mountain pass. The thing that lives in a particular old tree. They have no portfolios, no priesthoods, no doctrines. They have addresses. The sub-stratum provides the ambient numinous texture of the world -- the Skyrim-style enchanted feeling -- without requiring any deity to be real. A traveler crosses a pass and feels watched. A well produces water that tastes different on certain days. A tree that has stood for centuries drops a branch the day a notable person dies nearby. Whether these are spirits, coincidences, or natural phenomena is never settled. The four ambiguity devices apply at this level too, but they hardly need to -- the sub-stratum is already…

The largest and most internally diverse tradition family on the continent. Three civilizations -- Oravan, Ndjadi, and Irrah -- descend from a shared proto-theology that held the cosmos is ordered by the movement and division of waters: surface, underground, sky, dew, and the hidden moisture in living bodies. Ngaru-Bon touches the edge through dew/river rites whose relationship to the main complex is actively debated. The Substrate The Water-Covenant has no founder, no revealed text, no covenant moment. It is recoverable only by inference, like the Vedic substrate or Proto-Indo-European dyeus. In-world scholars disagree about whether it was ever a "religion" or only a shared cosmological grammar. The absence of a founding narrative is deliberate: it prevents any descendant tradition from claiming priority through apostolic succession. What the substrate left behind: - A tiered water cosmology -- the idea that different waters (rain, river, well, dew, bodily moisture) occupy different cosmological registers with different sacred valence - Purification rites tied to water-contact (washing, drinking, immersion, sprinkling) with register-specific protocols - A Tenth Water concept --…

The family documents how Veydrians actually lived, as distinct from the structures that governed them. The law layer records what the slavery grades were and how manumission worked; the economy layer records what each civilization traded and what it could not do without. This family records the rest: what a person ate, where they slept, what a bad year did to them, and what small moves let one rise. It is the texture the structural layers imply but never depict. The Family Remit is orthogonal to the control layers, not a duplicate of them. It reads and and shows where they land on a body. A file here earns its place only by adding lived texture that the legal and economic documents never see. It does not restate stratification grids, slavery grades, or commodity tables; it references them and moves on. The Asymmetric Frame Where a Veydrian institution carries a contested meaning, this family does not always hold the two readings as co-equal. The religion layer holds the practitioner and skeptic accounts of death as equally true because the afterlife is genuinely undecidable (ADR-0026). Poverty is different. Underclass: Casual wage-laborers, dockworkers, bankrupt factors, and destitute in-migrants of the Outer Quarters in the grain-import free-port. Who the Poor Are The Basin has no internal slavery, so its poverty is urban and wage-based. Day-laborers on the quays, dockworkers hired by the load, bankrupt factors, and destitute in-migrants from upstream civilizations make up the poor. The bottom of the bottom lives in the Outer Quarters at Dzong-Tamu, the slum that already appears in canon. A person falls by injury, blacklist, failed speculation, or simply by arriving faster than work appears. Daily Life and Subsistence Bread, watered wine, onions, and salted fish are the ordinary diet, and it rides the grain price. In a dearth the poor shift to coarse grains and foraged starch from the lagoon margins. Housing is a cramped tenement room shared by several families or a pallet in a confraternity hall. They own the clothes they stand in, a knife, perhaps a barrow or a set of hooks for unloading. Scarcity and Famine The Basin grows nothing; it is a clearing-house economy entirely dependent on imported grain. A bad harvest upstream, a blockaded river, or a disrupted caravan route spikes…

Underclass: Oasis sharecroppers, servile herders, and transient caravan porters who live below the documented caste tiers and outside the monopoly of water. Who the Poor Are Below the Imajīn, Ḥarrāb, Ghūlām, and Qalībin tiers and outside the Azmarāʔ caste stand the khammes, the fifth-share sharecroppers of the date-palm oases, and the bonded herders who tend camels they do not own. Above them in precarity are the caravan porters and water-carriers who service the routes Irrah controls. Caste endogamy and the water-monopoly fix their station as firmly as chains, even where the law stops short of calling them slaves. Daily Life and Subsistence The oasis garden is three-tiered: date palms above, fruit trees below, and cereals in the understory. The khammes household does the clearing, the channeling, and the hand-pollination of the palms, then takes one-fifth of the harvest. The herder lives on pastoral millet and camel-milk. Famine-foods are wild desert grass-seed and roasted locust, eaten in the very plagues that cause the dearth. A khammes family owns a few pots, a mattock, and the right to sleep in a mud-brick room that belongs to the landholder. Scarcity and Famine…

Underclass: Herders who have lost their stock to winter kill or misfortune and fallen into dependence at the settled margins of the steppe. Who the Poor Are The zhataq, the ones who lie down, are herders with too few animals to migrate and live as Kheshkai should. A man with fewer than five horses is compromised; a household that loses its breeding stock to a dzud must settle at the edge of a town or attach to a richer camp. This is downward mobility, not caste. A zhataq may have been a prosperous herder two winters ago; birth means nothing when the herd is gone. Daily Life and Subsistence Dairy, curds, and airag are rationed or absent. The poor eat marmot and other small game, wild onion, and traded millet bought with odd jobs. A patched and under-insulated ger is colder than the portable homes of the mobile camps, because the poor cannot afford new felt and cannot follow the herds to better pasture. Prime horses are too valuable to eat; they belong to the lender or the patron. Scarcity and Famine The dzud, the winter herd-kill, is the great catastrophe. A single bad winter of ice-crust and cold can annihilate a family's biological capital and leave them with nothing. Distress…

Underclass: River-plain laborers and craft families bound by interest-only pawn-debt to river-lords and merchants in a wealth-in-people economy. Who the Poor Are Below the documented noun-class tiers are the pawned, the nyamakala craft-castes, and the mosque mendicants. The pawned are usually children or young adults given as interest on a grain debt; the nyamakala are smiths, leatherworkers, and lower jeli whose endogamous trades fix their standing; the mosque poor are those who have no patron and survive on alms. In a society that counts wealth in people, to have no dependents and no master is the most exposed condition. Daily Life and Subsistence The ordinary meal is millet or sorghum porridge with baobab leaf and dried fish from the river. During the brief fertile window after the inundation families hoe the heavy black soil from dawn to dusk. Mud-brick and thatch houses cluster near the water; in the cities the poorest sleep in the mosque courtyards or in the lee of river warehouses. They own little beyond a hoe, a cooking pot, and the debts their parents contracted. Scarcity and Famine Multi-year drought is the recurring catastrophe, and unlike the highland states Ndjadi…

Underclass: Ore-haulers, coal-burners, forge-tenders, and other bonded laborers whose blood-price is a fraction of the elite rate and whose work is fixed by ritual-pollution doctrine. Who the Poor Are The polyandrous-lower-caste, perhaps three households in five, perform the heavy labor of the plateau mines and estates. Ore-haulers carry ingots down mountain tracks; forge-tenders breathe coal smoke and beat metal for the Inner-Council smith elite; disposal workers handle the dead and the waste that ritual doctrine declares impure. Below them all are the landless rationed servants tied to an estate. Their stong, the blood-price, is set at a fortieth of the elite rate, which is itself a measure of how little standing the law grants them. Daily Life and Subsistence The daily ration is barley tsampa and butter tea, enough to work but not enough to thrive. Bonded miners sleep in stone barracks or lean-tos near the workings; forge-tenders live in segregated quarters at the edge of the smith precinct. When the lord's stores are shut they dig wild tubers and nettles from the high slopes. Meat and good grain appear at festival times, usually as leftovers from the elite table. Scarcity…

Underclass: Fishing-village poor, debt-bonded cultivators, and indentured cove-labor trapped by a single fragile crop and monopsony spice pricing. Who the Poor Are Below the documented workshop-lineage hierarchy are the fishing poor of the outer coves, the debt-bonded and pawn-enslaved who work the spice gardens, and the indentured laborers of the cove works. The lived fact of Oravan poverty is dependence on one crop. A fishing household may eat, but it cannot pay taxes or bride-prices in fish; a spice cultivator may harvest, but he sells to the only buyer permitted by the workshop-lineage system. Daily Life and Subsistence Sago is the staple, starch-rich and protein-poor, supplemented by fish and coconut. An unsupplemented sago diet brings deficiency disease in a bad year. Houses are palm-thatch and bamboo, raised against the wet and the rats. The poor own nets, digging sticks, and small canoes; the workshop-lineage families own the drying sheds, the scales, and the contracts with the carrying-trade. Each of the seven civilizations makes its poor in a different way, and each tells a different story about why they are poor. This sub-layer documents the lived side of being poor: daily subsistence, how a bad year is survived, the informal economy and mutual-aid that hold the bottom together, the charity that reaches the destitute, and the narrow paths up. It does not restate the slavery grades, the manumission routes, or the stratification grids; those are the formal control layer (, ), and this sub-layer references them and moves to the texture they leave out. The Asymmetric Frame Every per-civ file carries two readings, but unlike the funerary layer they are not co-equal. The afterlife is undecidable, so the religion layer holds its two accounts in balance. Poverty is not undecidable. Underclass: Highland herders and laborers who have lost or never held ayllu kin ties, living on marginal land above the terraced valleys and dependent on the state storehouse. Who the Poor Are The waqcha, the kinless, sit below the documented lineage tiers of Qollari society. They are pushed to the highest and most barren elevations as marginal herders, or they labor as yanakuna retainers severed from their own kin. A person becomes waqcha by orphaning, by a household's collapse, by exile from an ayllu dispute, or by being born to a kin-severed mother. Without the ayllu there is no reciprocal labor pool, no marriage network, and no claim to the better terraces or water turns. Daily Life and Subsistence The day begins with chicha and a small portion of quinoa or potato. Meat is rare; when an alpaca dies or is slaughtered for ritual, the poor receive the offal and the tough cuts while the hanks of ch'arki go to the storehouse and the elite. The waqcha hut is a single room of fieldstone and adobe, roofed with ichu grass, often windowless and shared with the family's few animals through the coldest months. The Irrah medium pairs Mesopotamian clay tablets and seals with Nabataean caravan practice. Clay serves fixed archives; lighter media serve the road. How It Is Made Records are pressed into clay tablets at the mudbrick tower-cities. Caravan contracts and the ḥabal letter system travel on leather or skin. A carved cylinder or stamp authenticates a document, and one seal can authenticate many. Who Makes It and Controls Literacy Literacy is a craft held more widely than elsewhere. Irrah women are more frequently literate than men. Sacred Qalīb formulas remain oral-only, so writing one is desecration. What It Records Clay archives and sealed contracts hold the documentary core of the caravan economy: contracts, water-rights, debts, and the ḥabal letters that carry trust along the road. The seal makes each record authenticated and binding. What It Cannot Record The most sacred register deliberately stays off the most permanent medium. Clay is heavy and fixed, so it cannot travel easily. Portable contracts trade durability for mobility. Durability and Portability Fired clay is near-permanent and tamper-evident, and a sealed tablet resists forgery, which is the authority Irrah sells.…

The Qollari khipu pairs with the Inca cord-and-knot record. The analog is the technology and political economy of knotted-cord records, not any specific historical khipu. How It Is Made Spun and dyed camelid or cotton cords are knotted in positional clusters with color banding and seriation. The finished textile doubles as currency and record. Who Makes It and Controls Literacy The cords are cheap. The keeper is the cost. A hereditary record-keeper class holds the skill and the memorized oral keys that make a khipu readable. What It Records The medium is robustly quantitative. It encodes census, tribute-in-kind, stores, herds, land, military inventories, astronomy, and calendars. What It Cannot Record The khipu has two hard ceilings. It has no demonstrated narrative capacity, so it cannot record stories, law-as-prose, or argument. It is also not self-contained and needs its keeper's oral account. Durability and Portability Cords are physically durable and portable, but the record's survival is hostage to the keeper. The medium travels well yet remains fixed to a living human key. Politics of the Medium This is the medium paper most threatens. A khipu economy depends on an…

The Ngaru-Bon medium pairs Ethiopian Ge'ez and Tibetan monastic manuscript culture, monumental rock inscription, and Tibetan woodblock printing for sacred texts. How It Is Made Parchment and vellum come from treated animal skin. They are durable and expensive. Monastic scriptoria prepare and write them, and Dzong libraries hold the collections. Monumental stone inscription preserves imperial and sacred records. Woodblock prints sacred texts, the one reproduction technology that copies text rather than a mark. Who Makes It and Controls Literacy The monastic scribes hold the tightest literacy monopoly of the seven. The monastery is the archive, the school, and the block-printer of its sacred texts all at once. What It Records Parchment carries sacred and learned texts. Stone carries imperial and sacred records. Woodblock makes sacred texts reproducible, but only within the monastic frame. What It Cannot Record The medium is monastery-bound and expensive. It cannot circulate outside the monastic system, and its cost keeps volumes few. Durability and Portability Parchment is durable but expensive and monastery-bound. Stone is permanent but immovable. Woodblock prints sacred texts…

The Kheshkai medium pairs Scythian and Mongol oral epic with tamga brand-marks. History is sung poetry; tally-marks and clan-brands on leather and bone are the only written symbols. How It Is Made Knowledge is carried as epic sung poetry. Tally-marks and clan-brands on leather and bone are the only material records. Each horde has a unique brand, a reproducible identifying mark. Who Makes It and Controls Literacy There is no scribal class. The bard and brand carry memory. Literacy is near-absent and oral. Bards carry the sung history and shamans the religious memory, but neither is a record-keeping institution. What It Records The brand is identity and ownership; the tally is count; the epic is history. Together they handle lineage, herds, and martial memory without prose. What It Cannot Record It cannot record prose, contract, or argument. It has the lowest information ceiling of the seven. Durability and Portability Leather and bone are portable, and oral memory travels far, but the information ceiling is low. Politics of the Medium Kheshkai is least exposed to paper because it has almost no records to disrupt. The clan-brand is a reproduction technology: one carved object…

The Oravan medium pairs with Minoan Linear-A palace administration. How It Is Made The palace priesthood keeps trade and temple records in a syllabary on clay tablets and incised media. The palace economy collects and redistributes wealth, recording every flow. Who Makes It and Controls Literacy The priesthood controls the medium as an instrument of the redistributive palace economy. Literacy is palace-centered and priesthood-centered. Maritime and volcanic constraints keep the medium local. What It Records The tablets record administrative accounting, temple inventory, trade records, and the movement of goods through the palace. What It Cannot Record Clay tablets are durable but fixed. They are a poor fit for a far-trading thalassocracy, because sea-trade records cannot easily sail on clay. Durability and Portability The medium is durable but immovable. Its authority is tied to the palace archive, not to the ship or the distant port. Politics of the Medium An ocean-going trade league running on immovable palace tablets has a latent appetite for portable records. Oravan is therefore a plausible early adopter of paper for ship-borne contracts, even as the priesthood guards the…

Vaucresne rag paper pairs with the Arab and Chinese rag-pulp paper tradition and the westward paper road. How It Is Made Waste cloth is scoured, beaten to pulp, screen-formed into sheets, sized, and dried. The input is cheap and abundant wherever a textile economy exists. Who Makes It and Controls Literacy Craft workshops and guilds sell paper as a commodity. The surface is sold to anyone who can pay, decoupling the record from the record-keeping class. Literacy stays gated. What shifts is the gate, from trained scribe to the price of paper. What It Records It holds anything a script can write, at volume. Merchants and minor officials can keep books outside priestly or scribal archives. What It Cannot Record Paper has no inherent information ceiling; it holds whatever a script can write. Its limitation is fragility. It survives less well than parchment, clay, or stone, and that durability objection is the honest knock established orders raise. Durability and Portability Portability is high and cost is low. Paper travels well but must be stored carefully and recopied more often than heavy native media. The Ndjadi medium is a braided complex. It pairs Egyptian papyrus for pith-paper, South and Southeast Asian palm-leaf manuscript for bureaucracy, and Mesoamerican amate beaten-bark for the bark-scroll. All three are plant-fiber media, distinct from Vaucresne rag paper. How It Is Made Pith-paper comes from reed strips laid in layers and pressed. Palm-leaf is boiled, washed, dried, and flattened for writing. Bark-scroll is made from inner bark beaten and felted. Who Makes It and Controls Literacy The water-priest bureaucracy controls the medium. The hydraulic state runs on its ledgers, so record-keeping is an arm of the engineering-administrative priesthood. What It Records The complex serves ledgers, allocation tables, reservoir records, and distribution. Palm-leaf is the working surface; pith-paper is also exported. What It Cannot Record Tropical perishability is the main limit. Palm-leaf and pith decay in heat and humidity, so the bureaucracy must copy and recopy its records. Durability and Portability The media are lighter than clay or stone but less durable in wet heat; recopying is the price of portability. The Water-Covenant Substrate and the Divergence The deepest layer the comparative method can reach is a substrate of shared water-rites, roughly seventy generations back, with no political units that anyone today would recognize. The evidence is linguistic and gestural rather than monumental: a cognate root for oath surviving in three tongues, near-identical sunrise hydration rites among the peoples who became Oravan, Ndjadi, and Irrah, and three ritual postures held in common but weighted differently. Whether this was ever an organized religion or merely a shared cosmological grammar is disputed, and the dispute matters, because every living Water-Covenant tradition claims to preserve the original form. The substrate fractured along environmental lines into three descendants who took irreconcilable paths. Ndjadi grammaticalized the oath until it became a verb-tense, so that to speak in oath-tense casually is to bind oneself and the grammar is the religion. Oravan personalized it into a kin-relation with a named volcano-ancestor, from which the queen-church descends. Irrah codified it into a written instrument witnessed by specialists, so that the document is the oath. From the…

Stratigraphic Time The Veydrian past is a stratigraphic record, not a chronicle. There is no continental year-zero, no shared regnal list, and no surviving line of kings whose dates can be counted back. What survives instead is material: re-carved shrines where one people's totems overlie another's, cognate words that drifted apart in three directions, an inscription a recent earthquake pushed back into the light. The historian of Veydria works as a comparative linguist works on proto-Indo-European, reconstructing what must have stood beneath the divergent descendants, and as a Braudelian works on the longue durée, treating geography as the slow variable and politics as the fast. The continent measures elapsed time in generations, dynasties, and religious cycles, and these measures disagree. Kheshkai count in horse-generations and master-shaman transmissions, Ndjadi in flood-cycles and river-lord houses, Oravan in priestess-queen reigns, Qollari in calendar-keeper lineages. When a single event must be placed, the numbers diverge by a factor of two or three, and the divergence is not a flaw in the record. It is the record. What This File Is This is a worked example of a palimpsest kept in the reckoning of days. The re-carved shrines surface in stone and the disputed cognate in a word; this one surfaces in the count of the calendar itself. Two cloud-states in the southern Qollari range hold a calendar two weeks out of step with the unified Qollari reckoning, and they call the gap the Era of the Wrong Two Weeks, a name they wear as a banner rather than an apology. Like the re-carved shrines, the fracture is a layer of an older time showing through a newer one, and like them the two peoples who live with it read the same gap as opposite things. The offset is real and measurable to the day. What the gap means, whether it is fidelity to a pre-unification past or a schism that dressed itself in antiquity, is the open question, and the question is the content. The Scene The Qollari calendar is genealogy as much as astronomy. Dead lineages are fixed in the sky as stars and eclipse-positions, so that to correct the calendar is to revise the genealogical record and to move a day is to move an ancestor. What This File Is This is a worked example of a palimpsest read through language rather than stone, a single root that survives in all three Water-Covenant tongues with a slightly different shape and a wholly different function in each, so that the word itself is a buried layer showing through three descendant grammars at once. Like the Qhabal-Ur inscription, it implies a time before the three were separate, and like that inscription it cannot be made to say so without handing one tradition a victory the other two will not concede. The forms are real and the kinship between them is visible to anyone who lays them side by side. What the kinship means is the open question, and the question is the content. The Root and Its Three Shapes The root carries the sense of witness, the one who sees the oath sworn and can be called to say it was sworn. In Oravan, Tlhar- is an epithet, one of the names by which the Named One is addressed in the daughter-palace rites, the deity invoked as the seer who stands over every binding; it is a sacred word, seldom heard outside the rite. In Ndjadi, Tsar- is a particle, a verb-tense marker that places an utterance in the mode of having-been-witnessed,…

What This File Is This is a worked example of the most dangerous kind of palimpsest, the one whose buried layer, if it is a layer at all, would unsettle the account every living tradition gives of its own beginning. A small shrine somewhere in the Aethelian Basin uses a ritual posture found in none of the three living Water-Covenant traditions. The posture is real, and anyone trained in the rites can see that it belongs to none of them. Whether it is a local improvisation, a thing carried in from beyond the continent, or the last gesture of a fourth Water-Covenant line that died, is the open question. Unlike the Qhabal-Ur inscription, which every tradition is eager to read, this is the site scholars step around, because the third answer costs more than any of them wants to pay. The Scene The Water-Covenant rites bind an oath through the body, and each living tradition has its own stance for the binding. The Oravan address the Named One, the Ndjadi hold the witnessed-posture, the Irrah keep the witness-attendance, and each stance is as recognizable to a practitioner as a seal. What This File Is This is a worked example of a present-tense palimpsest, a site where an older layer of the past has surfaced into the playable present and every tradition reads it to its own advantage. It follows the structure of the Obsidian Blockade demonstration: a single event, multiple rational perspectives, no resolution. The inscription is real; its meaning is open; and the gap between the two is the content. The Scene Qhabal-Ur, the Drowned Step, sits at the center of the Aethelian Basin and has been the most contested sacred site on the continent for as long as the Basin has been a clearing house. A recent earthquake, within living memory, dropped a course of the old shrine wall and exposed a face of stone that had been buried beneath the floor. On it runs a single sentence that uses all three Water-Covenant grammatical forms at once: the Ndjadi oath-tense prefix, the Oravan deity-address, and the Irrah witness-formula, braided together in one line.
